episodes.title: Week 0–1: Hello, World
episodes.subtitle: Birth to day 7
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week zero to one, birth through day seven: hello, world. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This week at a glance.

The first week is about three things: feeding, warmth, and recovery. Babies are often alert for the first hour or two after birth, then very sleepy for a day or so. Many lose some weight in the first days. That is expected, and the AAP's guidance is that most babies regain birth weight by about ten to fourteen days. A loss of more than about ten percent is a signal for a closer look at feeding.

Expect a first pediatric visit around three to five days of age, often a day or two after leaving the hospital. Bring your feeding and diaper notes.

Jaundice, a yellow tint to the skin and eyes, is common and usually peaks around days three to five. It needs to be checked, not guessed at. Call if the yellow is spreading down the body, if your baby is very sleepy or not feeding well, or if you're unsure.

Chapter two. Senses and the growing brain.

Your baby sees best at about eight to twelve inches, the distance to your face during a feed. They prefer faces and bold contrast, and they already know your voice from the womb. Brief crossing or drifting of the eyes is common in the early months.

The best brain exercise this week is closeness. The AAP and the WHO support skin-to-skin contact right after birth and in the early days. It helps keep baby warm, steadies breathing and heart rate, and supports breastfeeding. Talk softly and let your baby study your face.

The natural lens. The WHO recommends delaying the first bath for at least twenty-four hours after birth, which matches what many natural-birth families prefer: leave the creamy vernix to soak in. Here the natural preference and the mainstream guideline agree.

Chapter three. Movement and tummy time.

Movements are reflexes: startle, grasp, rooting toward the breast, and stepping when held upright. Tummy time can begin soon after you get home. The AAP suggests starting with short supervised sessions and building toward fifteen to thirty minutes a day by about seven weeks. This week, a minute or two on your chest while you recline is plenty.

Chapter four. Feeding, four ways.

Four routes, kept separate, because a number from one should never become the benchmark for another.

Feeding at the breast. The first milk, colostrum, is small in volume and rich in antibodies. Milk usually comes in more fully between about days two and five. The CDC and AAP describe eight to twelve feeds in twenty-four hours, or about every two to three hours. Watch for early hunger cues like rooting and hands to the mouth. Diapers tell the story: one or two wet diapers in the first day or two, rising to about six or more by days five to six, and dark, sticky meconium turning to yellow stools by about day four or five. For context only, the Neville study from Denver in 1988 weighed directly nursed babies before and after every feed. Average daily intake was about four hundred eighty milliliters at day five and about five hundred sixty at day seven, with wide ranges. Those are thirteen families, not a target.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. If baby is separated or not latching, hand expression and pumping protect supply. In the Larkin study of mothers who exclusively pumped for babies in a NICU, average daily output climbed from about thirty milliliters on day one to over six hundred by day seven, but individual mothers ranged from almost nothing to over a liter. Those babies were preterm, so it's an indirect comparison. The Pumps tab shows your logged totals against that study. Bottle amounts this week are small, often one to two ounces, a range borrowed from formula guidance.

Formula. The AAP suggests about one to two ounces per feed in the first week, every two to three hours, and more only if baby is still showing hunger.

Mixed feeding. Log bottles in ounces and breast feeds as feeds. Don't add guessed ounces for the breast. If supplementing, ask your pediatrician or a lactation consultant how to protect supply.

The natural lens on formula. The FDA's Operation Stork Speed, part of the Make America Healthy Again effort, is reviewing formula nutrients for the first time since 1998 and expanding contaminant testing. Its latest results found most samples had low or non-detectable heavy metals. All legal U.S. formula must meet FDA nutrient standards. The FDA warns against homemade formula, including raw milk recipes.

Vitamin D. The AAP recommends four hundred international units a day for babies who get any breast milk, starting in the first days. A 2015 trial by Hollis and Wagner tested a maternal high-dose alternative, starting at four to six weeks. That's worth a conversation later with your pediatrician.

The parent's plate. Recovery takes fuel. Real-food dietitian Lily Nichols emphasizes protein, eggs, meat, fish, and broths after birth, and the 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines put real food at the center. Very low-carb eating while breastfeeding has been linked in case reports to a rare, serious condition called lactation ketoacidosis. Our reasoning: eat generously, drink to thirst, and don't fast this week.

The natural lens on the placenta. Some natural-birth families encapsulate the placenta. Evidence of benefit is limited, and the CDC has reported a case where placenta capsules were linked to a serious strep infection in a newborn. If you're considering it, talk with your clinician.

Chapter five. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Newborns sleep often, sixteen hours or more, in short stretches. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months.

The natural lens. Newborns don't have a day-night rhythm yet. Our reasoning: start the habit now with daylight and normal household sounds during the day, and dim, quiet night feeds. Keep babies under six months out of direct sun. Sunlight isn't a home treatment for jaundice; that needs a proper check.

Chapter six. Looking ahead.

Around two to three weeks, many babies have a growth spurt and want to cluster feed. Crying usually rises after about two weeks and peaks around six to eight weeks. The first social smile tends to appear around six to eight weeks. Teething usually starts around six months, solid foods start around six months with readiness signs, sitting alone falls between about four and nine months in the WHO motor study, and walking alone between about eight and eighteen months. Until about six months, only breast milk or formula: no water.

Chapter seven. What this means, and what to do.

First, feed often and watch diapers. They're the best clue you have this week.

Second, hold your baby skin-to-skin whenever you're awake and alert.

Third, keep the first pediatric visit, and ask about weight and jaundice.

Fourth, log by route, so your notes tell an honest story.

Fifth, the parent who gave birth is recovering too. Eat, drink, rest, and accept help.

When to call. If your baby is three months or younger and has a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, or higher, call your pediatrician right away, even if baby seems fine otherwise. Call too for fewer wet diapers than expected, yellow skin that's spreading or worrying, poor feeding, trouble breathing, blue lips, unusual sleepiness, or a stump with spreading redness. For the birthing parent, heavy bleeding, fever, a severe headache, chest pain, or thoughts of self-harm need urgent care. In an emergency, call nine one one.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from AAP HealthyChildren pages and its 2022 safe sleep report, the CDC, the WHO, the NHS, and the named studies: Neville 1988, Larkin 2013, and Hollis and Wagner 2015. Natural-lens material names its source and is opinion or emerging evidence unless we said otherwise. Links are in the Sources tab. This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. See you in week one.

episodes.title: Week 1: Finding Your Rhythm
episodes.subtitle: Days 7–14
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week one, days seven through fourteen: finding your rhythm. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This week at a glance.

This is the week most babies get back to birth weight. The AAP expects that by about ten to fourteen days. After that, many babies gain roughly two thirds of an ounce to an ounce a day in the early months. Your pediatrician watches the curve over time.

Feeding is still frequent, day and night, and it still doesn't look like a schedule. That's normal. Stools usually turn yellow and seedy for breastfed babies, and tan or yellow for formula-fed babies. The umbilical stump often falls off during this week or the next.

For the birthing parent, bleeding should be tapering, and the baby blues, tearfulness and mood swings, are very common in the first two weeks.

Chapter two. Senses and the growing brain.

Vision is still blurry beyond about a foot. Faces, black-and-white patterns, and slow movement draw attention. Hearing is good, and babies often calm to a familiar voice.

Brain exercise this week: talk to your baby during ordinary care. Say what you're doing as you change, bathe, and dress them. Harvard's Center on the Developing Child calls this back-and-forth serve and return. Your baby's glance or sound is a serve; your answer is the return. The CDC recommends no screen time before age two, other than video calls.

The natural lens. Magda Gerber's RIE approach treats even a newborn as a participant: tell the baby before you pick them up, and slow down during care. There isn't trial evidence for that specific method, but the reasoning fits what we know: calm, responsive, predictable care is what young babies need.

Chapter three. Movement and tummy time.

Arms and legs move in jerky, reflex patterns. Head control is minimal, so always support the head and neck.

Tummy time: two or three short sessions a day, a few minutes each, awake and watched, building toward the AAP's target of fifteen to thirty minutes a day by about seven weeks. Tummy-to-chest on a reclined parent is a gentle way to begin.

The natural lens. Natural-movement advocates favor floor time over swings and bouncers. The AAP agrees that limiting time in carriers and bouncers helps prevent flat spots.

Chapter four. Feeding, four ways.

Four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Eight to twelve feeds in twenty-four hours remains typical. Signs of enough: six or more wet diapers a day, regular yellow stools, and weight heading back to birth weight. A timer measures minutes, not milk. For context only, the Neville study, which weighed directly nursed babies before and after feeds, found an average of about five hundred sixty milliliters a day at day seven and about six hundred thirty at day fourteen, with wide ranges between babies. Thirteen families: context, not a target.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. Measured bottle amounts are real numbers, but there's no validated bottle-specific requirement at this age. Many babies take about two to three ounces per bottle, a range borrowed from formula guidance, so follow cues. Paced bottle feeding, with baby upright and pauses, is common lactation advice. Freshly expressed milk keeps up to four hours at room temperature and four days in the fridge, according to the CDC. In the Larkin exclusive-pumping study, average output from days seven to fourteen was roughly six hundred thirty to seven hundred fifty milliliters a day, with huge variation, in mothers of preterm babies. The Pumps tab shows that comparison.

Formula. AAP guidance is about two to three ounces per feed after the first week, every three to four hours, adjusted to cues.

Mixed feeding. Log bottles as measured and breast feeds as feeds. If bottles replace nursing sessions and you want to protect supply, pump around those times. A 2016 study by Kent found breastfeeding mothers who also pumped expressed a median of about a hundred sixty-eight milliliters a day, only part of their total production.

The natural lens on bottles and plastics. The AAP's 2018 policy on food additives advises not microwaving food or milk in plastic. Natural-living families often choose glass or stainless bottles, which is a reasonable, low-risk choice.

Vitamin D. The AAP recommends four hundred units a day for babies who get any breast milk. The 2015 Hollis and Wagner trial showed a maternal dose of sixty-four hundred units a day, starting at four to six weeks, kept babies' levels equal to infant drops. Ask your pediatrician if you'd like to consider it.

The parent's plate. The 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines emphasize real food, protein, and full-fat dairy. Lily Nichols adds a focus on eggs for choline, low-mercury fish for omega-3s, and red meat for iron. If you're low-carb, eat enough and avoid fasting; very low-carb diets while breastfeeding have been tied to rare cases of lactation ketoacidosis.

Chapter five. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Sleep comes in short stretches around the clock, often sixteen hours or more in total. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months.

The natural lens. Our reasoning: help the body clock develop by giving days light and noise, and nights darkness and quiet. A 2004 study by Yvonne Harrison found better night sleepers at six to twelve weeks got more early-afternoon light, a link, not proof. Keep babies under six months out of direct sun; window light and shade are plenty.

Chapter six. Looking ahead.

Coming soon: a growth spurt around two to three weeks, with more cluster feeding. Crying tends to rise and peak around six to eight weeks. The first social smile often appears around six to eight weeks. Further out: teething most often starts around six months, solids around six months with readiness signs, sitting alone between about four and nine months, and walking alone between about eight and eighteen months in the WHO motor study.

Chapter seven. What this means, and what to do.

First, celebrate regaining birth weight, and let weight and diapers, not the clock, guide you.

Second, keep tummy time short and frequent.

Third, narrate your day to your baby.

Fourth, log feeds by route.

Fifth, watch your own mood. Baby blues should ease within about two weeks. If sadness or anxiety lasts longer or feels heavy, call your clinician.

When to call. If your baby is three months or younger and has a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, or higher, call your pediatrician right away, even if baby seems fine otherwise. Call too for fewer wet diapers, poor feeding, yellow skin that's spreading or lasting past two weeks, pale stools, trouble breathing, or unusual sleepiness. In an emergency, call nine one one.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from AAP HealthyChildren pages and its 2022 safe sleep report and 2018 food additives policy, the CDC, the NHS, and the named studies: Neville 1988, Larkin 2013, Kent 2016, Hollis and Wagner 2015, and Harrison 2004. Natural-lens material names its source and is opinion or emerging evidence unless we said otherwise. Links are in the Sources tab. This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. See you in week two.

episodes.title: Week 2: The First Growth Spurt
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week two, days fourteen through twenty-one: the first growth spurt, and finding your feet. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This week at a glance.

By day fourteen, most healthy term babies are back to birth weight. The AAP expects that by about ten to fourteen days. From here, many babies gain roughly two thirds of an ounce to an ounce a day in the early months, but your pediatrician reads the growth curve over time, not one weigh-in.

Many families notice a growth spurt somewhere around two to three weeks. It often looks like a baby who suddenly wants to feed again and again, especially in the evening, and seems hard to settle. It usually passes in a few days, and it isn't, by itself, proof that milk is running out.

Crying also tends to climb from about two weeks and peak around six to eight weeks. A baby who cries more this week is usually doing something normal.

The umbilical stump usually falls off by about three weeks. Keep it clean and dry, and call for spreading redness, pus, or a foul smell.

Chapter two. Senses and the growing brain.

Vision at this age is blurry. Babies see best at about eight to twelve inches, roughly the distance to your face during a feed. They prefer high contrast and faces. Color vision develops over the first few months and is fairly good by about four to five months, so bold patterns beat pastels for now. It is also common for the eyes to drift or cross briefly. That is expected in the early months, but eyes that stay crossed or turned past about four months deserve a check.

Hearing is working, and familiar voices draw attention. The best brain exercise is what Harvard's Center on the Developing Child calls serve and return: baby makes a face, sound, or look, and you answer it. Narrate, sing, and hold eye contact in quiet alert moments. The CDC recommends no screen time before age two, other than video calls with family.

The natural lens. Montessori families often hang a black-and-white Munari mobile above a floor mat, and Magda Gerber's RIE approach favors calm attention and unhurried floor time over gadgets. Evidence for any particular mobile is thin, but the reasoning holds: contrast suits young eyes, and a calm face is the richest stimulus a newborn has.

Chapter three. Movement and tummy time.

Movements are mostly reflexes right now: startle, grasp, and stepping when held upright. They fade over the coming months.

Tummy time starts now. The AAP's 2022 safe sleep report says to begin supervised tummy time soon after coming home, and to build toward fifteen to thirty minutes total per day by about seven weeks. This week, think two or three sessions of a few minutes each, after a diaper change, while baby is awake and you are right there. Lying tummy-to-chest on a reclined parent counts as a gentle start.

The natural lens. Natural-movement advocates favor floor time over car seats, swings, and bouncers, and the AAP agrees that limiting time in carriers and bouncers helps prevent flat spots. If you babywear, keep the face visible, chin off the chest, and baby close enough to kiss.

Chapter four. Feeding, four ways.

We break feeding into four routes, because a number from one route should never quietly become the benchmark for another.

Feeding at the breast. The CDC and AAP describe eight to twelve feeds in twenty-four hours in the early weeks, and cluster feeding during a growth spurt is common. A nursing timer measures minutes, not milk. The signs of enough are steady weight gain, six or more wet diapers a day, and regular yellow stools. For context only, the Neville study from Denver in 1988 weighed directly nursed, exclusively breastfed babies before and after every feed. At day fourteen, the average was about six hundred thirty-four milliliters, or twenty-one ounces, in twenty-four hours, but individual babies ranged from about four hundred to nearly nine hundred milliliters. At day twenty-one, the average was similar. That was thirteen families: context, not a target.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. You have a measured number here, but no validated bottle-specific requirement for a two-week-old. Two to three ounces per bottle is a common early range borrowed from formula guidance, so treat it as a loose starting point and follow cues. Many lactation professionals recommend paced bottle feeding: baby fairly upright, bottle closer to horizontal, with pauses, so the flow feels more like the breast. That is professional practice more than trial evidence. If you're pumping, the Little Steps Pumps tab compares logged totals with an exclusive-pumping study and a separate full-supply reference. For storage, the CDC says freshly expressed milk is fine for up to four hours at room temperature and up to four days in the fridge.

Formula. AAP guidance is about two to three ounces per feed in these weeks, moving toward three to four ounces every three to four hours by the end of the first month. A rough planning guide is about two and a half ounces per pound of body weight per day, usually not more than about thirty-two ounces. Don't push a baby to finish.

Mixed feeding. Count bottle ounces as measured, and count breast feeds as feeds. Do not add a guessed number for the breast. If a bottle replaces a breast feed and you want to protect supply, lactation guidance is to pump around that time. In a 2016 study by Kent and colleagues, breastfeeding mothers who also pumped expressed a median of about a hundred sixty-eight milliliters a day, so pumped totals are only part of production.

The natural lens on formula. The FDA's Operation Stork Speed, part of the Make America Healthy Again effort, is reviewing formula nutrients for the first time since 1998, and its October twenty-ninth, 2026 testing update found most samples had low or non-detectable heavy metals. Many families in this movement prefer organic or whole-milk-fat formulas; all legal U.S. formula meets the same FDA nutrient standards, and the FDA warns against homemade or raw milk formula. On plastics, the AAP and natural voices agree: don't microwave milk or formula or heat it in plastic. Glass or stainless bottles are a reasonable choice.

Vitamin D. The AAP recommends four hundred international units a day for babies who get any breast milk, starting in the first days. The natural lens: a 2015 randomized trial by Hollis and Wagner, published in Pediatrics, found that mothers taking sixty-four hundred units a day supplied enough vitamin D through breast milk that their babies matched infants given drops. That trial started at four to six weeks postpartum. It's a real alternative to discuss with your pediatrician, not something to switch to on your own.

The parent's plate. A nursing mother needs roughly three hundred thirty to four hundred extra calories a day, according to the CDC. The new 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines put eating real food at the center, with protein at every meal and full-fat dairy, and that overlaps with what dietitian Lily Nichols, author of Real Food for Pregnancy, teaches about eggs, meat, fish, and nourishing whole foods after birth. If you eat low-carb, keto, or carnivore, there is one caution worth knowing. Case reports describe lactation ketoacidosis, a rare but serious condition, in breastfeeding women on very low-carb diets, especially with fasting or under-eating. Our reasoning: in these early weeks, eat enough, drink to thirst, don't fast, and talk with your clinician before going strictly ketogenic.

Chapter five. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Newborns sleep a lot, often sixteen hours or more, in short stretches day and night. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months.

The natural lens. Light sets the body clock. A 2004 study by Yvonne Harrison followed fifty-six babies at six, nine, and twelve weeks and found that babies who slept better at night were exposed to more light in the early afternoon. That's a link, not proof, but the reasoning is low-risk: bright days, dim nights. Feed by a window or sit outside in the shade by day, and keep night feeds dark and quiet. The AAP advises keeping babies under six months out of direct sun, so shade and window light are your tools for now. And sunlight is not a home treatment for jaundice.

Chapter six. Looking ahead.

Not on the agenda yet, but coming: the first social smile, usually around six to eight weeks. Teething, most often around six months, with a wide range. Rolling tummy to back, on the CDC's six-month list. Sitting alone, between about four and nine months in the WHO motor study, and walking alone, between about eight and eighteen months. Solid foods start around six months with signs of readiness. Until then, breast milk or formula is the whole menu: no water, no cereal in bottles.

Chapter seven. What this means, and what to do.

First, expect more feeding and fussing, and think growth spurt before anything else. Weight checks and diapers are your truth, not the clock.

Second, start tummy time: two or three short sessions a day, awake and watched.

Third, give the day bright light and the night darkness.

Fourth, log by route: bottles in ounces, breast feeds as feeds, pumping in the Pumps tab.

Fifth, eat real food and plenty of it, and don't fast while you're nursing.

Sixth, check on the parents. Baby blues usually ease within about two weeks of birth. Sadness or anxiety that lasts longer, or feels heavy, deserves a call to your own clinician. Help works.

When to call. If your baby is three months or younger and has a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, or higher, call your pediatrician right away. Call too for fewer wet diapers, poor feeding, trouble breathing, unusual sleepiness, green vomit, pale or white stools, or yellow skin that's spreading or still there past two weeks. In an emergency, call nine one one.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from AAP HealthyChildren pages and its 2022 safe sleep report, the CDC, the NHS, the WHO, and the named studies: Neville 1988, Kent 2016, Hollis and Wagner 2015, and Harrison 2004. Natural-lens material names its source and is opinion or emerging evidence unless we said otherwise. Links are in the Sources tab. This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. See you in week three.

episodes.title: Week 3: More Awake, More Opinionated
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week three, days twenty-one through twenty-eight: more awake, more opinionated. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This week at a glance.

Week three often brings longer stretches of quiet alertness: eyes open, scanning, calm. It also often brings a fussier evening. Many babies have a late-afternoon or evening window of crying and cluster feeding, and the overall crying curve is still rising toward its usual peak around six to eight weeks. That is normal development, not a sign you are doing something wrong.

Weight gain should be steady now that birth weight is regained, roughly two thirds of an ounce to an ounce a day for many babies. The one-month checkup is coming up. It's a good time to start a short list of questions.

Spit-up is very common. Most babies who spit up are what pediatricians call happy spitters: growing well, comfortable, and just messy. Small, effortless spit-ups after feeds are expected.

Chapter two. Senses and the growing brain.

Your baby's focus is still best at about eight to twelve inches, but you may notice longer gazes and brief tracking of a slowly moving face. High-contrast patterns and the human face remain the favorite things to look at. Color vision is developing and is fairly good by about four to five months.

Brain exercise for this week: copy your baby. When they open their mouth, open yours. When they make a sound, make it back. This is serve and return, the back-and-forth that Harvard's Center on the Developing Child describes as building the architecture of the brain. Read aloud, even adult books. What matters is your voice and rhythm. The CDC recommends no screen time before age two, except video calls.

The natural lens. Functional and natural-parenting voices emphasize skin-to-skin contact beyond the hospital days, for regulation, bonding, and breastfeeding. The mainstream evidence for skin-to-skin is strongest right after birth, but there's no downside to continuing it when you're awake and alert. Our reasoning: it costs nothing, and it's what your baby is built for.

Chapter three. Movement and tummy time.

Reflexes still lead the way. You may see a little more head lifting during tummy time, usually just for a moment and wobbly. That's the point: tummy time is strength training.

Keep building toward the AAP target of fifteen to thirty minutes total per day by about seven weeks. A practical week-three goal is three or four short sessions a day, a few minutes each, on a firm surface, awake and watched. If your baby protests, try a rolled towel under the chest, get down face to face, or do tummy-to-chest on a reclined parent.

The natural lens. Natural-movement advocates suggest a firm floor mat over bouncers and swings, and the AAP agrees that too much time in carriers and seats raises the risk of flat spots. Free floor time is a low-cost, low-risk habit, and the earlier it starts, the easier it is.

Chapter four. Feeding, four ways.

As always, four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Eight to twelve feeds in twenty-four hours is still the typical range, with cluster feeding in the evening. For context only, the Neville study from Denver in 1988, which weighed directly nursed, exclusively breastfed babies before and after every feed, found an average of about six hundred thirty milliliters, around twenty-one ounces, per day at day twenty-one, and about seven hundred fifty milliliters, around twenty-five ounces, at day twenty-eight. The range at day twenty-eight ran from under five hundred to over eleven hundred milliliters. That's thirteen families, so read it as context, not a goal. Your proof is weight and diapers.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. If you plan to use bottles, many lactation professionals suggest introducing one once breastfeeding is going well, often around three to four weeks. That's practical guidance, not a firm rule. There is still no validated bottle-specific requirement for this age. Many babies take roughly two to four ounces per bottle around now, but that range is borrowed from formula guidance, so follow cues. Use paced bottle feeding, and keep up the CDC storage rules: up to four hours at room temperature and four days in the fridge for fresh milk. The Little Steps Pumps tab shows logged pumping totals against an exclusive-pumping study and a separate full-supply reference, and it notes that the study ends at day fourteen.

Formula. AAP guidance moves toward about three to four ounces every three to four hours by the end of the first month. A rough guide is two and a half ounces per pound per day, usually capped around thirty-two ounces. Follow fullness cues: turning away, slowing down, relaxed hands.

Mixed feeding. Log bottle ounces as measured, and breast feeds as feeds. Don't add guessed ounces for the breast. If bottles are replacing nursing sessions and you want to keep your supply, pumping around those times helps signal your body to keep making milk.

Pacifiers. The AAP says offering a pacifier at sleep time is linked to a lower risk of SIDS, and for breastfed babies, to wait until breastfeeding is well established, often around three to four weeks. Never force it, and don't put it back in if it falls out during sleep.

The natural lens on spit-up. Integrative pediatrician Dr. Elisa Song, author of Healthy Kids, Happy Kids, argues against reaching quickly for acid-suppressing medicine for an infant's spit-up because of its possible effects on the gut microbiome. Mainstream pediatric gastroenterology guidance actually agrees: acid suppression isn't recommended for uncomplicated spit-up in a thriving baby. Shared first steps are smaller, more frequent feeds, burping, and keeping baby upright after feeds while awake.

The parent's plate. The new 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines put eating real food at the center, with protein at each meal and full-fat dairy. Real-food dietitian Lily Nichols emphasizes nutrient-dense staples like eggs for choline, fatty fish for omega-3s, and meat for iron and B12. If you eat low-carb or carnivore, keep calories up and don't fast. Lactation ketoacidosis is rare, but case reports tie it to very low-carb diets and under-eating while breastfeeding. Our reasoning is that a moderate approach is safer than a strict ketogenic one in these early weeks; talk with your clinician before going strict.

Chapter five. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Sleep is still scattered across day and night, often sixteen hours or more in total. The ABCs every time: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet on a firm, flat surface with nothing else in it. Room-share, don't bed-share, ideally for the first six months. Swaddling is fine if baby is placed on the back, the hips can move freely, and you stop once baby shows signs of trying to roll.

The natural lens. Babies aren't born with a working day-night rhythm; it develops over the first months. In Yvonne Harrison's 2004 study of babies at six to twelve weeks, better night sleepers got more early-afternoon light. That's a link, not proof, but the reasoning is low-risk: daytime naps in a bright room, a walk in the shade, and dark, quiet, boring night feeds. Keep babies under six months out of direct sun.

Chapter six. Looking ahead.

Coming soon: the first true social smile, usually around six to eight weeks; the CDC lists smiling when you talk on its two-month checklist. Cooing follows. Not yet: teething, most often around six months with a wide range; rolling, on the CDC's six-month list; sitting alone, between about four and nine months in the WHO motor study; and walking alone, between about eight and eighteen months. Solid foods start around six months with readiness signs. Until then, only breast milk or formula: no water, no cereal in bottles.

Chapter seven. What this means, and what to do.

First, plan for the evening fussy window. Line up help, dim the lights, and have a calming routine ready: feed, rock, sway, shush.

Second, keep tummy time growing: three or four short sessions a day.

Third, if bottles are part of your plan, this is a reasonable window to try one, with paced feeding.

Fourth, if spit-up isn't bothering your baby and weight is good, it's usually laundry, not illness.

Fifth, protect the day-night signal: bright days, dark nights.

Sixth, write down your questions for the one-month visit, including how you, the parents, are doing.

When to call. If your baby is three months or younger and has a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, or higher, call your pediatrician right away. Call too for forceful or projectile vomiting, green vomit, blood in spit-up or stool, poor weight gain, fewer wet diapers, trouble breathing, unusual sleepiness, or crying that seems like pain and won't settle. If you ever feel overwhelmed, put the baby down safely in the crib and step away for a few minutes. Never shake a baby. In an emergency, call nine one one.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from AAP HealthyChildren pages and its 2022 safe sleep report, the CDC, the WHO, and the named studies: Neville 1988 and Harrison 2004. Natural-lens material names its source and is opinion or emerging evidence unless we said otherwise. Links are in the Sources tab. This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. See you in week four.

episodes.title: Week 4: The One-Month Mark
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week four, days twenty-eight through thirty-five: the one-month mark. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This week at a glance.

Around one month, many babies are more alert, stay awake a little longer, and start to look intently at faces. The one-month well visit usually happens around now. Your pediatrician will check weight, length, and head size on the growth chart, and the AAP recommends that pediatricians also screen the birth parent for postpartum depression at these early visits. That's routine, and it's for you.

Crying is still climbing toward its usual peak at six to eight weeks. Many babies have a fussy evening window. When crying is long and intense in an otherwise healthy, growing baby, pediatricians may call it colic. A common definition is crying more than three hours a day, more than three days a week, for more than three weeks.

Chapter two. Senses and the growing brain.

Your baby may begin to follow a slowly moving face or toy briefly. Focus is still best at close range, and high-contrast patterns are still easiest. Color vision continues to develop and is fairly good by about four to five months.

Brain exercise for this week: face time, with no screen involved. Hold your baby about a foot from your face, make slow expressions, and pause. Wait for a response. That pause is the most important part of serve and return. Sing the same short songs every day; repetition builds familiarity.

The natural lens. Many natural-parenting families build days around being outdoors in the shade, with natural sounds and changing light, instead of screens or electronic toys. Our reasoning: that matches what the evidence does show, that young babies learn from people and real surroundings, not from screens. The CDC recommends no screen time before age two except video calls.

Chapter three. Movement and tummy time.

During tummy time, many babies now lift their head briefly and turn it from side to side. Hands are often fisted, with brief opening.

Keep building toward the AAP target of fifteen to thirty minutes total per day by about seven weeks. A practical goal this week is about ten to fifteen minutes total, in several short sessions. Get down at eye level. A mirror or a high-contrast card in front of baby helps.

The natural lens. Natural-movement voices like the RIE approach favor free floor time on a firm mat. Mainstream advice agrees that less time in seats and swings helps prevent flat spots and gives babies room to practice.

Chapter four. Feeding, four ways.

Four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Many babies still feed eight to twelve times a day, sometimes a bit fewer as they get more efficient. For context only, the Neville study from 1988, which weighed directly nursed babies before and after every feed, found an average of about seven hundred fifty milliliters, about twenty-five ounces, per day at day twenty-eight. The range ran from under five hundred to over eleven hundred milliliters. A larger 2023 review by Rios-Leyvraz and Yao gives an average of about six hundred twenty-five milliliters at one month for healthy, exclusively breastfed babies, but it mixes measurement methods and doesn't separate breast from bottle. The difference between those two numbers is a good reminder that these are study averages, not targets. Your proof is weight gain and diapers.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. Measured bottle amounts are real, but there's still no validated bottle-specific daily requirement at this age. Many babies take about three to four ounces per bottle around one month, a range borrowed from formula guidance. Paced feeding helps avoid overfeeding from a fast-flowing bottle. The CDC says frozen breast milk is best used within about six months, and up to twelve months is acceptable.

Formula. The AAP describes about three to four ounces every three to four hours by the end of the first month, roughly two and a half ounces per pound per day, usually capped around thirty-two ounces.

Mixed feeding. Log bottles as measured and breast feeds as feeds. Supply follows demand. If you're dropping breast feeds, do it gradually.

The colic question. Mainstream first steps are ruling out illness, soothing with motion, sound, and swaddling, and taking breaks. For babies who are breastfed, a 2018 Pediatrics meta-analysis by Sung and colleagues found the probiotic Lactobacillus reuteri, strain DSM 17938, reduced crying time by about twenty-five minutes a day. The benefit showed up in breastfed babies, not in formula-fed babies. That's an evidence-based option to discuss with your pediatrician. Some breastfeeding parents try removing cow's milk from their own diet for two to four weeks to see whether colic eases. The AAP mentions this as a reasonable trial for some babies, best done with your pediatrician's input.

Vitamin D, the natural lens. The AAP recommends four hundred units a day for babies who get breast milk. In the 2015 Hollis and Wagner trial, mothers who began sixty-four hundred units a day at four to six weeks postpartum produced milk that kept babies' vitamin D levels equal to babies given drops. This is the window when that option becomes relevant. Ask your pediatrician, and your own clinician, before switching.

The parent's plate. The 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines center real food, protein, and full-fat dairy. Functional medicine physicians like Dr. Mark Hyman emphasize whole foods and cutting ultra-processed foods and sugar, and functional practitioners often test vitamin D, iron, B12, and thyroid in postpartum fatigue. Mainstream doctors check thyroid and anemia too when fatigue or low mood persists. If you're doing low-carb or carnivore, keep calories and fluids up; case reports link very low-carb diets during breastfeeding to rare lactation ketoacidosis.

Chapter five. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Total sleep is often still fourteen to seventeen hours, and a slightly longer night stretch may appear. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months. Stop swaddling once baby shows signs of trying to roll.

The natural lens. Yvonne Harrison's 2004 study found that babies who slept better at night at six to twelve weeks got more early-afternoon light. That's a link, not proof, but a walk in the shade or a nap by a bright window costs nothing. Keep babies under six months out of direct sun.

Chapter six. Looking ahead.

Coming soon: the crying peak around six to eight weeks, and the first true social smile. The CDC's two-month checklist includes smiling when you talk, making sounds other than crying, and holding the head up during tummy time. Further out: teething most often starts around six months; solids around six months with readiness signs; rolling tummy to back by six months; sitting alone between about four and nine months, and walking alone between about eight and eighteen months in the WHO motor study.

Chapter seven. What this means, and what to do.

First, bring questions to the one-month visit, including your own mood and sleep.

Second, if evening crying is long and intense, plan a soothing routine and take turns. If it fits the colic pattern, ask about L. reuteri drops for a breastfed baby.

Third, aim for about ten to fifteen minutes of tummy time a day.

Fourth, if your baby is getting breast milk, settle the vitamin D plan: drops, or ask about the maternal option.

Fifth, eat enough real food, and keep logging by route.

When to call. If your baby is three months or younger and has a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, or higher, call your pediatrician right away, even if baby seems fine otherwise. Call too for crying that sounds like pain or comes with vomiting, fever, or poor feeding, blood in stool, fewer wet diapers, or poor weight gain. If you ever feel overwhelmed, put the baby down safely and step away. Never shake a baby. In an emergency, call nine one one.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from AAP HealthyChildren pages, the CDC, the WHO, and the named studies: Neville 1988, Rios-Leyvraz and Yao 2023, Sung 2018, Hollis and Wagner 2015, and Harrison 2004. Natural-lens material names its source and is opinion or emerging evidence unless we said otherwise. Links are in the Sources tab. This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. See you in week five.

episodes.title: Week 5: Toward the Crying Peak
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week five, days thirty-five through forty-two: toward the crying peak. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This week at a glance.

Week five often brings two things at once: more fussing, and the first glimpses of real connection. Crying in healthy babies usually peaks around six to eight weeks and then declines, often noticeably by three to four months. Researchers who study infant crying, including pediatrician Ronald Barr, describe this as a normal developmental curve. The Period of PURPLE Crying program, created to prevent shaken baby syndrome, explains it to parents: crying that peaks, is unexpected, resists soothing, looks like pain, is long-lasting, and often happens in the evening.

Many babies also start to smile in response to faces around now. If you haven't seen it yet, that's normal; the CDC puts it on the two-month checklist.

Chapter two. Senses and the growing brain.

Eyes follow faces more smoothly. Babies may begin to coo, making soft vowel sounds. They startle at loud sounds and calm to familiar voices.

Brain exercise for this week: conversation. When your baby coos, coo back, then pause. Babies learn the rhythm of conversation long before words. Read a picture book with bold images, and talk about what you see.

The natural lens. Natural-parenting families often favor singing, rhythm, and being carried over electronic soothers. Our reasoning: that's consistent with the research on serve and return, which centers on people, not devices.

Chapter three. Movement and tummy time.

During tummy time, many babies lift their head for a few seconds and may push briefly on their forearms. Head control when held upright is still developing, so keep supporting the head.

Aim for fifteen minutes or more total per day, working toward the AAP target of fifteen to thirty minutes by about seven weeks.

The natural lens. Babywearing is popular in natural parenting and can calm a fussy baby. If you use a carrier or wrap, follow the TICKS checklist from UK sling safety groups: tight, in view at all times, close enough to kiss, keep the chin off the chest, and a supported back. Carriers aren't for sleep surfaces at home; transfer a sleeping baby to the crib.

Chapter four. Feeding, four ways.

Four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Feeds may start to spread out a little, but cluster feeding and evening comfort nursing are common, especially around a six-week growth spurt. A timer measures minutes, not milk. Steady weight gain and plenty of wet diapers are the signs that matter. Studies of exclusively breastfed babies show daily intake stays fairly stable from about one month to six months: the 2023 Rios-Leyvraz and Yao review averages about six hundred twenty-five milliliters at one month and about seven hundred thirty at three and six months, with wide individual variation. Babies don't need dramatically more milk each month. They need roughly the same amount, used for a growing body.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. That stable-intake pattern is useful for planning, but it comes from breastfeeding research, so treat it as indirect for bottles. Many babies take about three to four ounces per bottle around now, a range borrowed from formula guidance. Paced bottle feeding helps babies stop when full.

Formula. Formula-fed babies often increase toward four ounces per feed. The AAP's planning guide is about two and a half ounces per pound per day, generally not more than about thirty-two ounces. Unlike breast milk, formula volume does tend to rise with weight.

Mixed feeding. Count measured bottles, count breast feeds, and don't add guessed ounces. If you're planning a return to work, now's a good time to build a small freezer stash with one extra pump a day.

The colic question, natural lens. Some families take a colicky baby to a chiropractor or osteopath. A 2012 Cochrane review of manipulative therapies for infant colic found the evidence was weak and too limited to recommend them. If you go, choose someone experienced with infants, and don't let it delay a medical check for a baby who seems unwell. The probiotic L. reuteri has better evidence for breastfed babies; ask your pediatrician.

The parent's plate. The 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines emphasize real food and protein at each meal. Real-food dietitian Lily Nichols stresses nutrient density after birth: eggs, meat, fish, liver in moderate amounts, and vegetables. Very low-carb diets while breastfeeding have been linked to rare lactation ketoacidosis in case reports; eat enough and don't fast.

Chapter five. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Total sleep is often fourteen to seventeen hours, with the longest stretch perhaps three to four hours. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months.

The natural lens. Evening crying often peaks just as daylight fades. Our reasoning: a bright, active morning and early afternoon, then a dim, calm evening, may help the body clock. Yvonne Harrison's 2004 study linked more early-afternoon light to better night sleep at six to twelve weeks. That's correlation, but it's low-risk to try.

Chapter six. Looking ahead.

Coming next: the crying peak, the social smile, and cooing. By two months, the CDC lists looking at your face, smiling when you talk, reacting to loud sounds, holding the head up on the tummy, and opening the hands briefly. Further out: teething around six months on average; solids around six months with readiness signs; sitting alone between about four and nine months, and walking alone between about eight and eighteen months in the WHO motor study.

Chapter seven. What this means, and what to do.

First, expect the crying peak. Crying is not a sign that you're failing.

Second, make a plan for overwhelm. Put the baby down safely in the crib, step away, breathe, and call someone. Never shake a baby.

Third, keep tummy time going, aiming for fifteen minutes or more a day.

Fourth, if you babywear, use TICKS.

Fifth, if work is coming, start a small milk stash and try a bottle with paced feeding.

When to call. Call too for crying that is high-pitched or unusual for your baby, crying with fever, vomiting, or poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, or a baby who is hard to wake. In an emergency, call nine one one.

episodes.title: Week 6: Smiles and the Six-Week Peak
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week six, days forty-two through forty-nine: smiles and the six-week peak. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This week at a glance.

Week six is famous for two reasons. First, crying in healthy babies often reaches its peak somewhere around six to eight weeks. Second, many babies start offering real social smiles, the kind that answer your face. Both are normal, and both can happen on the same day.

Many families also notice another growth spurt around six weeks: a day or two of frequent feeding and fussiness. It usually passes.

For the birthing parent, this is often around the time of a postpartum checkup. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists now recommends contact within the first three weeks and a full postpartum visit no later than twelve weeks, so timing varies. Bring questions about recovery, mood, sleep, pelvic floor, exercise, and contraception.

Chapter two. Senses and the growing brain.

Babies now track a moving face more smoothly and may watch you walk across the room. Cooing is starting. Color perception is improving, and babies may show more interest in bright colors, though contrast still wins.

Brain exercise for this week: the smile game. Get face to face, smile, talk in a warm, sing-song voice, and wait. When your baby smiles or coos, respond with delight. That loop of serve and return builds early social and language circuits.

The natural lens. Natural-parenting families often prefer real faces and voices over toys that light up and talk. Our reasoning: a baby's attention is limited, and the best use of it is you.

Chapter three. Movement and tummy time.

Many babies lift their head higher during tummy time, sometimes to about forty-five degrees, and may push up briefly on their forearms. The AAP target is fifteen to thirty minutes total per day by about seven weeks, so this is the week to get there. The World Health Organization's 2019 guidelines go further, recommending at least thirty minutes on the tummy spread through the day for babies who aren't yet mobile.

The natural lens. Floor time on a firm mat, with a parent nearby, is the natural-movement default. Mainstream agrees: limit time in seats, swings, and bouncers.

Chapter four. Feeding, four ways.

Four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Expect a growth-spurt surge, then a return to your normal pattern. Many babies feed somewhere around seven to ten times a day at this age. Remember that human milk intake in exclusively breastfed babies stays fairly stable from one to six months, averaging roughly six hundred to seven hundred fifty milliliters in the 2023 Rios-Leyvraz and Yao review. A surge in feeding usually means the baby is asking for a supply bump, not that milk has failed.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. If you pump, output may respond to the extra demand. Bottle amounts of about three to five ounces are common, a range borrowed from formula guidance; follow cues and use paced feeding. Watch for the baby who finishes a bottle fast and still seems hungry; a slower nipple or more pauses may help more than a bigger bottle.

Formula. Many babies take about four to five ounces per feed. Stay near the AAP guide of about two and a half ounces per pound per day, usually not more than about thirty-two ounces.

Mixed feeding. During a growth spurt, nursing more often is the natural way to raise supply. If you're supplementing, ask a lactation consultant how to time pumping so supply keeps up.

The parent's plate. Appetite often returns with a vengeance around now. The 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines emphasize protein at every meal and real, minimally processed food. Many parents want to lose pregnancy weight. A gradual pace, often described as about a pound a week, is commonly cited as compatible with milk supply. If you're returning to low-carb or keto, our reasoning is to ease in, keep calories and fluids adequate, and avoid fasting while you're exclusively breastfeeding; case reports tie very low-carb diets during breastfeeding to rare lactation ketoacidosis. Real-food dietitian Lily Nichols recommends prioritizing protein, fat, and nutrient-dense foods over strict restriction in this period.

Chapter five. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Night sleep may begin to consolidate, but many babies still wake every two to four hours to feed. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months.

The natural lens. Yvonne Harrison's 2004 study tracked babies at six, nine, and twelve weeks. Babies who slept well at six weeks tended to sleep well later, and better night sleepers were exposed to about twice as much early-afternoon light. It's observational, but the practical step is easy: get daylight between midday and late afternoon, in the shade, and keep evenings dim. For your own sleep, morning daylight is a common circadian tip from sleep researchers too.

Chapter six. Looking ahead.

The crying peak should start to ease over the next several weeks, often noticeably by three to four months. The two-month checklist from the CDC includes smiling when you talk, cooing, looking at a toy for several seconds, and holding the head up on the tummy. Further out: teething usually starts around six months, solids around six months with readiness signs, rolling tummy to back by six months, sitting alone between about four and nine months, and walking alone between about eight and eighteen months in the WHO motor study.

Chapter seven. What this means, and what to do.

First, smile back. The social smile is your baby's first conversation.

Second, ride out the crying peak with a plan, a partner, and breaks.

Third, hit the tummy-time target: fifteen to thirty minutes a day in short sessions.

Fourth, during a growth spurt, feed more often before assuming supply has dropped.

Fifth, book or keep your own postpartum visit, and if you're changing your diet, ease in.

When to call. If your baby is three months or younger and has a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, or higher, call your pediatrician right away, even if baby seems fine otherwise. Call too for crying that is unusual, high-pitched, or comes with fever, vomiting, or poor feeding; fewer wet diapers; or a baby who seems floppy or hard to wake. For the parent, persistent sadness, anxiety, or intrusive thoughts deserve a call; help works. In an emergency, call nine one one.

This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. See you in week seven.

episodes.title: Week 7: Hands, Coos, and the Tummy-Time Goal
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week seven, days forty-nine through fifty-six: hands, coos, and the tummy-time goal. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This week at a glance.

By about seven weeks, many babies are more social, more vocal, and stronger. The AAP's tummy-time target, fifteen to thirty minutes a day, is meant to be reached around now. Babies begin to notice their hands, and the startle and grasp reflexes slowly soften.

Crying may still be at or near its peak, but the end is in sight. Many families find evenings get easier over the next month.

If a parent is returning to work in the coming weeks, this is a good time to plan childcare, pumping, and bottles.

Chapter two. Senses and the growing brain.

Babies now watch moving people and objects, and many briefly look at their own hands. They coo and may make gurgling sounds. They turn toward sounds and voices.

Brain exercise for this week: describe and pause. Show your baby a simple object, like a red cup. Name it, move it slowly, and let them look. Then pause and see what they do. Short, calm play beats long, busy play.

The natural lens. Montessori-inspired families often keep a few simple, real objects within view rather than a pile of toys, and the RIE approach encourages letting babies explore freely on the floor. Evidence for these specific methods is thin. The reasoning, less clutter and more attention, matches what we know about how babies learn.

Chapter three. Movement and tummy time.

During tummy time, many babies hold their head up for longer and may push up on their forearms. When on their back, they kick and wave with more control.

You've reached the AAP target if you're at fifteen to thirty minutes a day. The WHO recommends at least thirty minutes a day for babies who aren't yet mobile. Keep sessions short and frequent; stop when your baby is done.

The natural lens. Natural-movement advocates suggest barefoot, unrestricted floor time, with loose clothing. That's harmless and lets babies feel the floor.

Chapter four. Feeding, four ways.

Four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Many babies feed seven to ten times a day. Feeds may be quicker as babies get more efficient. Shorter feeds don't mean less milk.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle, and return-to-work planning. A rule of thumb used by many lactation professionals is about one to one and a quarter ounces of breast milk for each hour a baby is away from the breastfeeding parent. That's practical guidance, not a validated requirement, and it comes from the idea that intake is fairly stable from one to six months. Babies taking expressed milk often take about three to five ounces per bottle. Pump about as often as the baby would feed. Label milk with the date, use the oldest first, and follow CDC storage rules: four hours at room temperature, four days in the fridge, and best within six months frozen.

Formula. Many babies take about four to five ounces per feed, roughly two and a half ounces per pound per day, usually not more than about thirty-two ounces in total.

Mixed feeding. If you're returning to work, keep nursing when you're together, morning, evening, and weekends, and pump during separation. That helps protect supply.

The natural lens on formula and water. Some families worry about fluoride when mixing powdered formula. The CDC says using fluoridated tap water is safe, and that if you're concerned about mild tooth spotting called fluorosis, you can sometimes use low-fluoride bottled water. Whichever water you use, follow the label for safe preparation. And the FDA's Operation Stork Speed recently reported most formula samples had low or non-detectable heavy metals.

The parent's plate. The 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines center real food, protein, and full-fat dairy. Functional medicine physicians like Dr. Mark Hyman push the same direction, whole foods and fewer ultra-processed foods and added sugars, which fits a busy parent planning meals ahead. Batch-cook proteins and keep easy foods like eggs, yogurt, and nuts nearby.

Chapter five. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

The longest night stretch may grow to four or five hours for some babies; others still wake every few hours. Both are normal. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months. Stop swaddling at the first signs of trying to roll.

The natural lens. Our reasoning on light: a consistent wake-up time, daylight during the day, and a dim, calm bedtime routine may help the body clock settle. Harrison's 2004 study links early-afternoon light to better night sleep, an observational link, not proof.

Chapter six. Looking ahead.

Next month, cooing becomes more conversational, head control improves, and babies may start batting at toys. The CDC's four-month list includes chuckling, holding the head steady without support when held, holding a toy put in the hand, and bringing hands to the mouth. Teething most often starts around six months, solids around six months with readiness signs, sitting alone between about four and nine months, and walking alone between about eight and eighteen months.

Chapter seven. What this means, and what to do.

First, celebrate the tummy-time goal, and keep it fun.

Second, offer simple objects and your face, not screens.

Third, if work is coming, make a pumping and bottle plan using the one-ounce-per-hour rule of thumb as a starting point.

Fourth, if you use formula, choose water thoughtfully and follow preparation instructions.

Fifth, simplify your own eating with batch-cooked real food.

When to call. If your baby is three months or younger and has a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, or higher, call your pediatrician right away, even if baby seems fine otherwise. Call too for a baby who isn't feeding well, has fewer wet diapers, is unusually sleepy or floppy, or doesn't seem to respond to sounds or look at faces. In an emergency, call nine one one.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from AAP HealthyChildren pages, the CDC, the WHO's 2019 guidelines, the FDA, and the named studies: Rios-Leyvraz and Yao 2023 and Harrison 2004. This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. See you in week eight.

episodes.title: Week 8: The Two-Month Checkpoint
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week eight, days fifty-six through sixty-three: the two-month checkpoint. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This week at a glance.

Two months is a milestone checkpoint. The CDC's list of what most babies do by two months, meaning at least three out of four babies, includes: calming when spoken to or picked up, looking at your face, seeming happy to see you, smiling when you talk or smile, making sounds other than crying, reacting to loud sounds, watching you as you move, looking at a toy for several seconds, holding the head up during tummy time, moving both arms and legs, and opening the hands briefly.

If your baby isn't doing one or two of these yet, it's a conversation, not an emergency. The CDC's advice is simple: you know your child best, so share concerns early with your pediatrician.

The two-month well visit usually happens around now. Bring your list and your feeding notes.

Chapter two. Senses and the growing brain.

Vision is sharpening. Babies follow objects further across their field of view and show more interest in color. Eyes that drift occasionally are still common; eyes that are constantly crossed or turned after about four months deserve a check.

Brain exercise for this week: take turns talking. When your baby coos, copy the sound, then wait. The CDC suggests exactly this: copy your baby's sounds and see how long the back-and-forth lasts. Hold a rattle off to one side and see if your baby looks for the noise.

The natural lens. Natural-parenting families often limit screens in the room, not just for the baby. The CDC agrees: being responsive is easier when your own screen time is limited around the baby.

Chapter three. Movement and tummy time.

Many babies can lift their head during tummy time and may push up on their forearms. Hands open more, and arm movements are smoother.

Keep tummy time at fifteen to thirty minutes or more each day, in several sessions. Put a toy or mirror at eye level in front of your baby.

The natural lens. Natural-movement advocates favor time on the floor over gear. The AAP agrees that limiting time in carriers and bouncers helps prevent flat spots.

Chapter four. Feeding, four ways.

Four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Many babies now feed about seven to nine times a day. Feeds can be shorter and more efficient. Human milk intake in exclusively breastfed babies stays relatively stable from one to six months, so there isn't a big jump in volume to expect, just a growing, more efficient baby. Weight checks at the two-month visit are the best measure.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. Bottle amounts of about four to five ounces are common, a range borrowed from formula guidance. There's no validated bottle-specific requirement. If your baby regularly takes much larger bottles than you'd expect and spits up a lot, slow the flow and pause more.

Formula. Many babies take about four to five ounces per feed. The AAP planning guide is about two and a half ounces per pound per day, usually capped around thirty-two ounces. Formula-fed babies who get about thirty-two ounces a day get enough vitamin D from formula.

Mixed feeding. Count measured bottles and breast feeds separately. If supply feels lower, more frequent nursing or pumping is the main lever.

Vitamin D, the natural lens. If your baby gets breast milk, the AAP recommends four hundred units a day of vitamin D. The 2015 Hollis and Wagner trial found mothers taking sixty-four hundred units a day kept babies' levels the same as infant drops. Either path can work; just pick one with your pediatrician.

The parent's plate. The 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines put real food, protein, and full-fat dairy at the center. Lily Nichols highlights choline from eggs and omega-3 fats from low-mercury fish while breastfeeding. Iodine matters too: the National Institutes of Health lists a higher iodine need during lactation, and if you avoid iodized salt, ask whether you need a supplement.

Chapter five. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Some babies sleep a longer first stretch at night, sometimes four to six hours. Others still wake often. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months.

The natural lens. Babies begin producing their own rhythmic melatonin over the first months. Our reasoning: daylight in the day and darkness at night help that system along. Harrison's 2004 study linked more early-afternoon light at six to twelve weeks to better night sleep. Keep babies under six months out of direct sun.

Chapter six. Looking ahead.

By four months, the CDC lists chuckling, cooing back, turning toward your voice, holding the head steady when held, holding a toy, swinging at toys, bringing hands to the mouth, and pushing up onto elbows on the tummy. Teething usually starts around six months, with a wide range. Rolling tummy to back is on the six-month list. Solids start around six months with readiness signs. Sitting alone falls between about four and nine months, and walking alone between about eight and eighteen months, in the WHO motor study.

Chapter seven. What this means, and what to do.

First, use the CDC two-month list as a guide, not a test, and bring questions to the well visit.

Second, play turn-taking games with sounds every day.

Third, keep tummy time steady.

Fourth, if your baby gets breast milk, confirm the vitamin D plan.

Fifth, keep eating real food, and check your iodine.

When to call. If your baby is three months or younger and has a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, or higher, call your pediatrician right away, even if baby seems fine otherwise. Call too if your baby isn't responding to loud sounds, isn't watching faces, seems floppy or very stiff, isn't feeding well, or has lost a skill. In an emergency, call nine one one.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from the CDC's milestone checklists, AAP HealthyChildren pages, the NIH, and the named studies: Rios-Leyvraz and Yao 2023, Hollis and Wagner 2015, and Harrison 2004. Natural-lens material names its source and is opinion or emerging evidence unless we said otherwise. Links are in the Sources tab.
