episodes.title: Week 9: Conversations Begin
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week nine, days sixty-three through seventy: conversations begin. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This week at a glance.

Around nine weeks, many babies are clearly social. They smile, coo, and seem to enjoy back-and-forth. Crying usually starts to ease after the six-to-eight-week peak. Many babies discover their hands and watch them with fascination.

Some babies show early signs of trying to roll. The AAP says to stop swaddling as soon as a baby shows signs of attempting to roll, and that can come earlier than parents expect.

Chapter two. Senses and the growing brain.

Babies now follow objects through a wider arc and can look from one object to another. Color perception continues to develop. Hearing is sharp; babies often turn toward voices.

Brain exercise for this week: the conversation game. Talk to your baby, pause, and let them answer with coos. Copy their sounds. Read simple board books with bold pictures. The amount of back-and-forth talk in the first years is linked to later language skills, and you can't overdo warm, responsive talk.

The natural lens. Natural-parenting families often prefer singing, rhymes, and stories to electronic media. That aligns with the CDC: no screen time before age two except video calls.

Chapter three. Movement and tummy time.

During tummy time, many babies hold their head up steadily and may push up on their forearms. On their back, they may bat at a toy dangling overhead.

Keep tummy time at thirty minutes or more a day if your baby enjoys it, as the WHO recommends for babies not yet mobile. Offer a toy just out of reach to encourage head turning and reaching.

The natural lens. A firm floor mat, minimal gear, and lots of supervised floor time are the natural-movement default. If your baby tilts the head to one side or you notice a flat spot, mention it to your pediatrician; early repositioning and tummy time help.

Chapter four. Feeding, four ways.

Four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Many babies feed about seven to nine times a day. Some drop a night feed; others don't. Both are normal. Growth is judged on the growth chart, not ounces.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. Bottles of about four to five ounces are common, a range borrowed from formula guidance. For return-to-work planning, many lactation professionals use a rule of thumb of about one to one and a quarter ounces per hour of separation. That's practical guidance, not a requirement. Pump about as often as the baby feeds.

Formula. Many babies take about four to six ounces per feed, roughly two and a half ounces per pound per day, usually not more than about thirty-two ounces.

Mixed feeding. If daycare bottles are coming, try a few bottle feeds from another caregiver ahead of time. Paced feeding helps a breastfed baby accept the bottle without overfeeding.

The natural lens on formula. Many families in the natural and Make America Healthy Again space prefer organic formula, formulas made with whole-milk fat, or those without corn syrup solids. The FDA's Operation Stork Speed is reviewing formula nutrients and carbohydrate sources, and its latest contaminant testing found most samples low or non-detectable. All legal U.S. formula meets FDA nutrient standards. Don't make homemade formula; the FDA warns that it can cause serious harm.

The parent's plate. The 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines emphasize real food and protein at each meal. If you eat low-carb, keto, or carnivore, know that there's little research on how those diets affect breast milk, and that very low-carb diets during breastfeeding have been linked to rare lactation ketoacidosis in case reports, especially with fasting or intense exercise. Our reasoning: keep some carbohydrate, eat enough, and don't fast while exclusively breastfeeding.

Chapter five. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Many babies have a longer first stretch of sleep. Total sleep is often around fourteen to sixteen hours. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months. Stop swaddling once there are signs of rolling.

The natural lens. Harrison's 2004 study tracked babies at nine weeks too. Better night sleepers had more early-afternoon light. Our reasoning: a daily walk in the shade after lunch is a low-risk habit worth trying.

The bed-sharing debate. Some natural-parenting families bed-share. Anthropologist James McKenna of the University of Notre Dame argues that for sober, nonsmoking, breastfeeding mothers, what he calls breastsleeping is a normal human pattern. The AAP disagrees and recommends against bed-sharing, because the risk of sleep-related death is higher. Both sides agree on the most dangerous situations: sleeping with a baby on a sofa or armchair, after alcohol or sedating medicines, with smoking, with a preterm or very young baby, or in soft bedding. The safest place for your baby to sleep is a separate, flat, bare crib or bassinet in your room. If you might fall asleep while feeding, do it in your bed, not a sofa, with pillows and blankets away from the baby, and move baby back to the crib when you wake.

Chapter six. Looking ahead.

By four months, the CDC lists laughing or chuckling, cooing back, holding the head steady when held, holding a toy, swinging at toys, and pushing up onto the elbows. Teething most often starts around six months; drooling can start earlier and doesn't always mean teeth are coming. Solids start around six months with readiness signs. Sitting alone falls between about four and nine months, and walking alone between about eight and eighteen months.

Chapter seven. What this means, and what to do.

First, talk with your baby, and leave space for answers.

Second, stop swaddling at the first sign of rolling.

Third, keep up daily floor time.

Fourth, plan daycare bottles with paced feeding and a realistic per-hour estimate.

Fifth, if you're eating low-carb, eat enough and keep some carbs.

When to call. If your baby is three months or younger and has a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, or higher, call your pediatrician right away, even if baby seems fine otherwise. Call too if your baby doesn't respond to sounds, doesn't watch faces, can't hold the head up at all during tummy time, or has lost a skill. In an emergency, call nine one one.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from AAP HealthyChildren pages and its 2022 safe sleep report, the CDC, the WHO, the FDA, and the named study: Harrison 2004. Natural-lens material names its source and is opinion or emerging evidence unless we said otherwise. Links are in the Sources tab. This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. See you in week ten.

episodes.title: Week 10: Reaching Out
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week ten, days seventy through seventy-seven: reaching out. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This week at a glance.

Around ten weeks, many babies start reaching toward the world. They may swipe or bat at a dangling toy, and their hands open more often. Smiles come easily, and cooing may sound more like conversation. Crying, for most families, is easing from its peak.

This is also a common time for a parent to go back to work, so routines are shifting. Babies often adapt better than parents expect, especially when caregivers are responsive and feeding plans are clear.

Chapter two. Senses and the growing brain.

Vision is improving quickly. Babies can follow a toy from side to side and are starting to coordinate eyes and hands. Color vision is developing; bright, saturated colors attract attention.

Brain exercise for this week: reach and name. Hold a bright toy within reach, let your baby swipe, and name what happened: you touched the ball. Then let them rest. Read a short book every day, pointing at pictures. The CDC suggests talking, reading, and singing as everyday brain builders, with no screens before age two except video calls.

The natural lens. Montessori families often use a simple hanging toy, like a ring or bell on a ribbon, over a floor mat at this stage, so babies can practice batting. Evidence for the specific toy is thin; the reasoning is that babies need chances to practice reaching, and a simple setup gives them that. Always supervise, and keep cords out of reach.

Chapter three. Movement and tummy time.

Many babies hold their head up well during tummy time and push up on their forearms. Some begin rocking or rolling slightly to the side. On their back, they kick strongly and may bring their hands together.

Keep tummy time going, thirty minutes or more a day spread out, as the WHO recommends for babies not yet mobile. Try side-lying play with a rolled towel behind the back to encourage reaching across.

The natural lens. Natural-movement advocates encourage barefoot floor play and minimal time in containers like car seats outside the car, bouncers, and swings. Mainstream advice agrees that container time should be limited.

Chapter four. Feeding, four ways.

Four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Many babies feed about six to nine times a day, and feeds may be quick. Babies get easily distracted during feeds now; a quiet, dim room can help. Intake in exclusively breastfed babies stays fairly stable from one to six months.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. Bottles of about four to six ounces are common, a range borrowed from formula guidance. If daycare reports your baby is taking much more than you pump, ask caregivers to use paced feeding, a slow-flow nipple, and to stop at fullness cues. The rule of thumb of about one to one and a quarter ounces per hour of separation is a practical starting point, not a requirement.

Formula. Many babies take about four to six ounces per feed, roughly two and a half ounces per pound per day, usually capped around thirty-two ounces.

Mixed feeding. With work and daycare, many families shift to mixed feeding. Keep breastfeeding when together, and pump during separation to protect supply. Count bottles as measured and breast feeds as feeds.

The parent's plate, natural lens. Low-carb and carnivore physicians like Dr. Ken Berry argue for cutting refined sugar and highly processed foods, and many low-carb voices also argue against industrial seed oils. The new 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines also push hard against highly processed foods and added sugars, so here mainstream and natural advice overlap. The seed-oil question itself is debated, and evidence is mixed; we label that as an open question. For a nursing parent, the practical takeaway is the same: build meals around protein, real fats, vegetables, and enough total food, and don't fast.

Chapter five. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Many babies have one longer sleep stretch at night, and some are starting to settle into a few predictable naps. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months.

The natural lens. Our reasoning: keep wake-up time roughly consistent, get daylight after lunch, and keep the hour before bed dim and calm. Harrison's 2004 study, which followed babies to twelve weeks, linked more early-afternoon light to better night sleep. It's correlation, but it's low risk.

Chapter six. Looking ahead.

By four months, the CDC lists chuckling, turning toward your voice, holding the head steady when held, holding a toy, swinging at toys, bringing hands to the mouth, and pushing up onto elbows on the tummy. Rolling tummy to back is on the six-month list. Teething most often starts around six months, solids around six months with readiness signs, sitting alone between about four and nine months, and walking alone between about eight and eighteen months.

Chapter seven. What this means, and what to do.

First, give your baby chances to reach: simple toys, close by, supervised.

Second, keep floor time and tummy time a daily habit.

Third, make feeding plans clear for caregivers, including paced bottle feeding.

Fourth, build your own meals around real food, protein, and enough of it.

Fifth, keep a consistent wake time and daylight in the afternoon.

When to call. If your baby is three months or younger and has a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, or higher, call your pediatrician right away, even if baby seems fine otherwise. Call too for poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, a baby who doesn't follow moving things with the eyes or doesn't respond to sounds, or one who seems very floppy or very stiff. In an emergency, call nine one one.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from AAP HealthyChildren pages, the CDC, the WHO, the 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines, and the named studies: Rios-Leyvraz and Yao 2023 and Harrison 2004. Natural-lens material names its source and is opinion or emerging evidence unless we said otherwise. Links are in the Sources tab. This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. See you in week eleven.

episodes.title: Week 11: Strong Arms, Round Heads
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week eleven, days seventy-seven through eighty-four: strong arms, round heads. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This week at a glance.

Around eleven weeks, many babies are pushing up during tummy time, holding their heads more steadily, and making a wider range of sounds. Some may let out their first laugh soon; the CDC's four-month checklist includes chuckling.

Drooling often increases around now. That usually reflects developing salivary glands and mouthing, not necessarily teething. First teeth most often appear around six months.

This is also a good week to look at your baby's head shape. Flat spots, called positional plagiocephaly, can develop when babies spend a lot of time lying in the same position. Tummy time and repositioning help.

Chapter two. Senses and the growing brain.

Babies now look at faces and objects for longer, follow movement smoothly, and may recognize familiar people from across the room. They respond to tone of voice.

Brain exercise for this week: copy and stretch. Copy your baby's sound, then add a new one. They coo ah, you say ah-boo. Play simple peekaboo with a cloth. Read and sing daily.

The natural lens. Natural-parenting families often emphasize time outdoors, in the shade, with natural sounds and changing light, as sensory input. Our reasoning: varied real-world input, with a caring adult narrating, is what babies are built to learn from.

Chapter three. Movement and tummy time.

Many babies push up on their forearms and hold their head and chest up for a while. Some start to roll partway onto a side. On their back, they bring hands together and to the mouth.

Head-shape check. Look down at your baby's head from above. If one side looks flatter, or the head always turns the same way, alternate the direction your baby faces in the crib, alternate which arm you hold them in, and increase supervised tummy time. Mention it at the next visit; most mild flat spots improve with repositioning.

The natural lens. Natural-movement advocates frame flat spots as a sign of too much container time: car seats used outside the car, swings, bouncers, and loungers. The AAP's guidance is similar. Babies should always sleep on their back, but awake time should include plenty of tummy time and fewer containers.

Chapter four. Feeding, four ways.

Four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Many babies feed about six to eight times a day. Distractibility is common; feed in a quiet space if needed. Some babies start sleeping a longer night stretch and feed more during the day.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. Bottles of about four to six ounces are common, a range borrowed from formula guidance. Babies don't need bigger bottles every week, because intake in breastfed babies is fairly stable from one to six months.

Formula. Many babies take about four to six ounces per feed, about two and a half ounces per pound per day, usually not more than about thirty-two ounces. Formula volume tends to rise with weight.

Mixed feeding. Keep a balance that protects supply if you want to keep breastfeeding: nurse when together, pump when apart.

The natural lens on gut health. Integrative pediatrician Dr. Elisa Song emphasizes protecting the infant gut microbiome, through breast milk when possible, avoiding unnecessary antibiotics and acid-suppressing medicines, and later, a diverse diet. Mainstream medicine agrees that antibiotics should be used only when needed and that acid suppression isn't recommended for uncomplicated spit-up. Breast milk contains prebiotic sugars called human milk oligosaccharides that feed beneficial bacteria; that part is well established.

The parent's plate. The 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines emphasize real food. Many breastfeeding parents continue a prenatal vitamin. Lily Nichols emphasizes choline from eggs, iodine, vitamin D, and omega-3s from low-mercury fish. If you're low-carb, eat enough and don't fast.

Chapter five. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Many babies sleep about fourteen to sixteen hours in total, with a longer night stretch. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months.

The natural lens. Our reasoning on rhythm: light in the morning and early afternoon, dim lights in the evening, and a short, repeatable bedtime routine: feed, bath or wipe-down, song, crib. Harrison's 2004 study linked early-afternoon light to better night sleep at six to twelve weeks.

Chapter six. Looking ahead.

By four months, the CDC lists chuckling, holding the head steady without support when held, holding a toy, swinging at toys, bringing hands to the mouth, pushing up onto the elbows on the tummy, and opening the mouth when hungry at the sight of breast or bottle. By six months: rolling tummy to back, reaching for toys, and laughing. Teething usually starts around six months, solids around six months with readiness signs, sitting alone between about four and nine months, and walking alone between about eight and eighteen months.

Chapter seven. What this means, and what to do.

First, check your baby's head shape and vary positions.

Second, keep tummy time generous and container time short.

Third, play copy-and-stretch sound games.

Fourth, protect the gut: breast milk if possible, and avoid unnecessary medicines.

Fifth, keep a simple bedtime routine.

When to call. If your baby is three months or younger and has a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, or higher, call your pediatrician right away, even if baby seems fine otherwise. Call too for a head shape that's worsening, a head that always tilts or turns one way, poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, or a baby who doesn't respond to sounds or faces. In an emergency, call nine one one.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from AAP HealthyChildren pages and its 2022 safe sleep report, the CDC, and the named studies: Rios-Leyvraz and Yao 2023 and Harrison 2004. Natural-lens material names its source and is opinion or emerging evidence unless we said otherwise. Links are in the Sources tab. This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. See you in week twelve.

episodes.title: Week 12: End of the Fourth Trimester
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week twelve, days eighty-four through ninety-one: the end of the fourth trimester. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This week at a glance.

Three months is often called the end of the fourth trimester. Many babies are now more predictable, more social, and less fussy. Crying has usually eased from its peak. Many babies hold their heads more steadily, laugh or chuckle, and bring their hands to their mouths.

This week also opens the door to the monthly episodes in Little Steps. From here on, each episode covers a month, with week-by-week expectations inside.

Chapter two. Senses and the growing brain.

Babies follow faces and objects smoothly, look from one thing to another, and are starting to see color well; color vision is fairly good by about four to five months. Depth perception develops a bit later, over the next few months.

Brain exercise for this week: give your baby a voice. Narrate what you think they're feeling: you're looking at the window, you hear the dog. Pause after questions. Read every day. Hold a rattle to one side and let your baby find the sound.

The natural lens. Natural-parenting families often keep toys simple: a rattle, a soft ball, a wooden ring, and a mirror. The reasoning is that fewer, simpler toys invite more exploration, and it costs less. Evidence for one toy over another is thin.

Chapter three. Movement and tummy time.

Many babies push up on their forearms during tummy time, hold their head steady when held upright, and may swing at toys. Some begin rolling from tummy to back; the CDC lists that on its six-month checklist, so earlier is a bonus, not a requirement.

Once rolling begins, never leave your baby on a bed, couch, or changing table, even for a second.

The natural lens. Floor time on a firm mat remains the natural-movement priority. Mainstream advice agrees: plenty of supervised floor time and limited container time.

Chapter four. Feeding, four ways.

Four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Many babies feed about six to eight times a day. The 2023 Rios-Leyvraz and Yao review found an average of about seven hundred thirty milliliters a day at three months in healthy, exclusively breastfed babies, but individual babies vary widely and the review mixes measurement methods. Your baby's growth curve is the real measure.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. Bottles of about four to six ounces are common, a range borrowed from formula guidance. Because intake is fairly stable from one to six months, pumped-milk needs usually don't climb much from here.

Formula. Many babies take about four to six ounces per feed, often around twenty-four to thirty-two ounces a day, using the AAP guide of about two and a half ounces per pound per day and a cap of about thirty-two ounces.

Mixed feeding. Count measured bottles, count breast feeds, and don't add guessed ounces.

Looking ahead to iron. The AAP recommends that exclusively breastfed babies start an iron supplement of one milligram per kilogram per day at four months, until iron-rich foods are part of the diet. Formula is fortified with iron. The natural lens: many families in this space would rather meet iron needs with food, and meat and egg yolk are iron-rich first foods. But solids aren't recommended until around six months, so the four-to-six-month gap is a real question to discuss with your pediatrician.

Solids, a preview. The AAP, CDC, and WHO recommend starting solids around six months, not before four months, when babies show readiness signs: sitting with support, good head control, interest in food, and the ability to move food to the back of the mouth instead of pushing it out. Not yet. No cereal in bottles.

The parent's plate. Keep eating real food. If you're returning to low-carb or keto, ease in, keep calories adequate, and avoid fasting while exclusively breastfeeding.

Chapter five. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Many babies sleep about fourteen to sixteen hours in total. Some begin sleeping longer stretches at night; others don't yet, and that's normal. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months.

The natural lens. Harrison's 2004 study found babies who slept well at six weeks tended to sleep well at twelve, and that better sleepers had more early-afternoon light. Our reasoning: keep the light rhythm going. A sleep shift often happens around four months, so a steady routine now helps.

Chapter six. Looking ahead.

Coming in month three and four: laughing, cooing back, holding a toy, swinging at toys, bringing hands to the mouth, and pushing up on the elbows. By six months: rolling tummy to back, reaching, and blowing raspberries. Teething most often starts around six months, with a wide range. Sitting alone falls between about four and nine months, and walking alone between about eight and eighteen months in the WHO motor study.

Chapter seven. What this means, and what to do.

First, enjoy a more social, predictable baby.

Second, never leave your baby on a raised surface.

Third, ask your pediatrician about iron at four months if your baby is exclusively breastfed.

Fourth, learn the readiness signs for solids, but wait for them.

Fifth, keep the light-and-dark rhythm steady.

When to call. If your baby is three months or younger and has a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, or higher, call your pediatrician right away, even if baby seems fine otherwise. Call too for poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, or a baby who doesn't follow faces, doesn't respond to sounds, or has lost a skill. In an emergency, call nine one one.

episodes.title: Month 3: Laughter and Hands
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month three, from three to four months, roughly weeks thirteen through seventeen: laughter and hands. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This month at a glance.

The fourth trimester is behind you. Most babies are now more predictable and more social, and crying has usually eased from its six-to-eight-week peak. This month is about hands, laughter, and stronger necks. By four months, the CDC's checklist includes smiling on their own to get your attention, chuckling, cooing back, turning toward your voice, holding the head steady when held, holding a toy put in the hand, swinging at toys, bringing hands to the mouth, and pushing up onto the elbows during tummy time.

Chapter two. Week by week this month.

Week thirteen: many babies chuckle or laugh for the first time. Tickles, silly sounds, and peekaboo are favorites.

Week fourteen: hands come together in the middle and go to the mouth constantly. Mouthing is how babies explore; keep small objects out of reach.

Week fifteen: batting turns into swiping and then grabbing. Many babies hold a rattle briefly when you put it in their hand.

Week sixteen: during tummy time, some babies push up on their forearms with their chest off the floor and may roll from tummy to back by accident. Never leave your baby on a raised surface.

Week seventeen: many families notice a sleep shift around four months, often called the four-month sleep regression. Sleep is maturing to include more adult-like cycles, so babies may wake more between cycles for a few weeks. It's development, not a setback.

Chapter three. Senses and the growing brain.

Color vision is fairly good by about four to five months, and depth perception is developing. Babies follow moving objects smoothly and look from one thing to another. They recognize familiar faces and voices.

Brain exercise for this month: conversation with gaps. Talk, pause, and let your baby answer. Copy their sounds. Read every day; point at pictures and name them. Babies learn language from responsive people, not screens. The CDC recommends no screen time before age two except video calls.

The natural lens. Natural-parenting families often value time outdoors, with natural sounds and light, and simple toys over electronic ones. Our reasoning: varied, real-world sensory input with a caring adult is a sound bet, though there's no trial comparing toy types.

Chapter four. Movement and tummy time.

Keep tummy time at thirty minutes or more a day if your baby enjoys it, as the WHO recommends for babies who aren't yet mobile. Put toys just out of reach to encourage reaching and pivoting. Side-lying play builds reaching across the body.

The natural lens. Natural-movement advocates encourage floor time over containers and baby gear. Mainstream advice agrees: limit time in seats, swings, and bouncers, both for development and to prevent flat spots.

Chapter five. Feeding, four ways.

Four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Many babies feed about six to eight times a day and may be easily distracted. The 2023 Rios-Leyvraz and Yao review found an average of about seven hundred thirty milliliters a day at three months in healthy, exclusively breastfed babies, roughly the same as at one month or six months. That means breastfed babies don't need dramatically more milk as they grow during these months.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. Bottles of about four to six ounces are common, a range borrowed from formula guidance. Because intake is stable, pumped-milk needs usually stay steady. Use paced feeding and slow-flow nipples, and keep up CDC storage rules.

Formula. Many babies take about four to six ounces per feed, often twenty-four to thirty-two ounces a day. The AAP guide is about two and a half ounces per pound per day, usually capped around thirty-two ounces.

Mixed feeding. Count measured bottles and breast feeds separately. If supply dips after a return to work, more frequent pumping or nursing is the main lever.

Iron at four months. The AAP recommends that exclusively breastfed babies start an iron supplement of one milligram per kilogram per day at four months, until they eat iron-rich foods. Formula is iron-fortified. The natural lens: many families would rather meet iron needs with food, and meat and egg yolk are iron-rich. But solid foods are generally recommended around six months, so talk with your pediatrician about the gap.

Solids, not yet. The AAP, CDC, and WHO recommend around six months, and not before four months. Readiness signs include good head control, sitting with support, interest in food, and losing the tongue-thrust reflex. No cereal in bottles.

The parent's plate. The 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines center real food, protein, and full-fat dairy. If you're returning to low-carb, keto, or carnivore, ease in, eat enough, and avoid fasting while exclusively breastfeeding. Case reports link very low-carb diets during breastfeeding to rare lactation ketoacidosis.

Chapter six. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Total sleep is often about fourteen to sixteen hours, with two to four naps. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months. Stop swaddling once your baby shows signs of rolling.

The natural lens. Our reasoning: around the four-month sleep shift, a strong day-night signal may help. Get daylight in the morning and early afternoon, in the shade, and keep evenings dim and calm. Harrison's 2004 study linked early-afternoon light to better night sleep in babies up to twelve weeks. It's correlation, but it's low risk.

Chapter seven. Looking ahead.

By six months, the CDC lists rolling from tummy to back, pushing up with straight arms, leaning on hands to sit, reaching to grab, blowing raspberries, laughing, and closing lips to show they don't want more food. Teething most often starts around six months, with a wide range. Solids start around six months with readiness signs. Sitting alone falls between about four and nine months, crawling on hands and knees between about five and thirteen and a half months, and walking alone between about eight and eighteen months in the WHO motor study.

Chapter eight. What this means, and what to do.

First, laugh with your baby. It's a milestone and a gift.

Second, keep raised surfaces off-limits; rolling can surprise you.

Third, ask about iron at four months if your baby is exclusively breastfed.

Fourth, learn the solids readiness signs, but wait for them.

Fifth, expect a sleep shift around four months, and keep the routine steady.

When to call. Under three months, a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, means calling your pediatrician right away. From three to six months, the AAP says to call for a fever of one hundred one, or thirty-eight point three Celsius, or higher. Call too if your baby doesn't follow moving things, doesn't respond to sounds, can't hold the head up, doesn't bring hands to the mouth, or has lost a skill. In an emergency, call nine one one.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from the CDC's milestone checklists, AAP HealthyChildren pages, the WHO, and the named studies: Rios-Leyvraz and Yao 2023 and Harrison 2004. Natural-lens material names its source and is opinion or emerging evidence unless we said otherwise. Links are in the Sources tab. This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. See you in month four.

episodes.title: Month 4: The Great Solids Debate
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month four, from four to five months, roughly weeks seventeen through twenty-one: the great solids debate. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This month at a glance.

Four-month-olds are busy. Many hold their head steady, push up on their elbows, grab toys, laugh, and bring everything to their mouth. Some roll. Many are going through a sleep shift. And many parents start hearing very different advice about when to begin solid foods. This month we'll lay out both sides carefully.

Chapter two. Week by week this month.

Week seventeen: the four-month sleep shift is common. Sleep cycles are maturing, so night waking may increase for a few weeks.

Week eighteen: many babies reach and grab with more accuracy and pass a toy between hands.

Week nineteen: rolling tummy to back, and sometimes back to tummy, may begin. Babies push up with straighter arms.

Week twenty: drooling and chewing on hands are common. That doesn't always mean teeth are coming, but some babies get their first teeth this early.

Week twenty-one: babies may sit with support and look around with interest at mealtimes. Watching you eat isn't the same as being ready to eat.

Chapter three. Senses and the growing brain.

Color vision is fairly good by about four to five months, and depth perception is developing, which helps reaching. Babies respond to their name more often and to changes in your tone of voice.

Brain exercise for this month: name things. When your baby looks at something, name it. Play peekaboo. Read board books every day. The CDC suggests responding to your baby's sounds and copying them, and no screen time before age two except video calls.

Chapter four. Movement and tummy time.

Keep tummy time daily, thirty minutes or more if your baby enjoys it. Encourage rolling by placing toys to one side. On the back, babies may grab their feet.

The natural lens. Natural-movement advocates encourage barefoot, free floor play. That fits mainstream advice. Avoid baby walkers; the AAP warns they cause injuries and don't help walking.

Chapter five. Feeding, four ways, and the solids question.

Four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Many babies feed about five to eight times a day. Intake in exclusively breastfed babies is fairly stable from one to six months. Distractibility is common; a quiet room helps.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. Bottles of about four to six ounces are common, a range borrowed from formula guidance.

Formula. Many babies take about four to six ounces per feed, often twenty-four to thirty-two ounces a day. The AAP guide is about two and a half ounces per pound per day, usually capped around thirty-two ounces.

Mixed feeding. Count measured bottles and breast feeds separately.

Iron. The AAP recommends an iron supplement of one milligram per kilogram per day starting at four months for exclusively breastfed babies, until iron-rich foods are eaten. Formula is iron-fortified. Ask your pediatrician.

Now the solids debate. The mainstream baseline: the AAP, CDC, WHO, and the 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines recommend breast milk or formula as the only food for about the first six months, with solids introduced around six months when the baby shows readiness. The AAP says not before four months. Readiness signs: good head and neck control, sitting with support, interest in food, opening the mouth for a spoon, and moving food to the back of the mouth instead of pushing it out.

The natural lens. The Weston A. Price Foundation, a prominent voice in traditional, nutrient-dense eating, suggests a soft-cooked egg yolk with a pinch of salt as early as four months, and cod liver oil from around four months. Here's an honest look at those claims. Egg yolk is nutrient-dense, and current allergy guidance actually encourages introducing egg early when solids begin. But the mainstream advises against added salt for babies, because infant kidneys handle sodium poorly. Cod liver oil is high in vitamin A, and too much vitamin A can be harmful, so dosing matters; don't give it without your pediatrician's input, and don't double up with other vitamin A or D supplements. The Foundation also advises delaying egg whites until one year, which conflicts with current allergy research.

Allergy prevention. The LEAP trial, published in 2015, found early peanut introduction cut peanut allergy dramatically in high-risk babies. U.S. guidelines now say babies with severe eczema or egg allergy may benefit from peanut introduction as early as four to six months, after talking with their pediatrician, who may test first. For most babies, peanut and egg can be introduced when solids start, around six months.

Our reasoning, labeled as reasoning: for most families, waiting for clear readiness signs, usually close to six months, then starting with nutrient-dense, iron-rich foods like egg and meat, satisfies both the mainstream evidence and the natural lens. If your baby has severe eczema or a food allergy, talk to your pediatrician now about peanut and egg.

The parent's plate. Keep eating real food and enough of it. The 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines emphasize protein, whole foods, and fewer highly processed foods.

Chapter six. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

During the four-month shift, babies may wake more often. A consistent, short bedtime routine helps. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months. Once your baby can roll both ways, it's okay to let them find their own position, but always place them on the back to start.

The natural lens. Our reasoning: keep a strong day-night signal. Daylight in the morning and afternoon, and a dim, calm evening.

Chapter seven. Looking ahead.

By six months, the CDC lists rolling from tummy to back, pushing up with straight arms, leaning on hands while sitting, reaching to grab, blowing raspberries, laughing, and closing lips to show they're done. Teething most often starts around six months. Sitting alone falls between about four and nine months, crawling between about five and thirteen and a half months, and walking alone between about eight and eighteen months.

Teething prep. When teeth come, the AAP suggests a clean finger to rub the gums, or a chilled, not frozen, teething ring. The FDA warns against teething necklaces, bracelets, and amber beads, which can cause choking and strangulation, and against benzocaine gels for teething. Teething does not cause a true fever.

Chapter eight. What this means, and what to do.

First, watch for readiness signs; don't start solids just because of age or a birthday on the calendar.

Second, if there's severe eczema or a food allergy, talk with your pediatrician about early peanut and egg.

Third, if you're interested in the Weston Price approach, discuss egg yolk timing, salt, and cod liver oil with your pediatrician first.

Fourth, ask about iron if your baby is exclusively breastfed.

Fifth, skip baby walkers and teething jewelry.

When to call. Under three months, a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, means calling your pediatrician right away. From three to six months, the AAP says to call for a fever of one hundred one, or thirty-eight point three Celsius, or higher. Call too if your baby can't hold the head steady, doesn't reach for toys, doesn't respond to sounds, or has lost a skill. In an emergency, call nine one one.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from the CDC, AAP HealthyChildren pages, the WHO, the FDA, the 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines, NIAID's peanut guidelines, and the LEAP trial. The natural lens draws on the Weston A. Price Foundation's published infant-feeding guide. Natural-lens material names its source and is opinion or emerging evidence unless we said otherwise. Links are in the Sources tab. This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. See you in month five.

episodes.title: Month 5: Rolling and Getting Ready
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month five, from five to six months, roughly weeks twenty-one through twenty-six: rolling and getting ready. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This month at a glance.

Month five is a month of preparation. Many babies roll, reach and grab accurately, sit with support, and put everything in their mouth. Many watch your food with great interest. By the end of the month, many babies are close to ready for solid foods, and families start planning first foods. This episode sets up that plan, comparing the mainstream baseline with the nutrient-dense, natural lens.

Chapter two. Week by week this month.

Week twenty-one: rolling tummy to back is common, and some babies roll back to tummy.

Week twenty-two: babies reach with one hand and transfer toys from hand to hand.

Week twenty-three: sitting with support improves. Many babies lean forward on their hands, called tripod sitting.

Week twenty-four: babbling may add consonant sounds, and blowing raspberries is a favorite.

Week twenty-five and twenty-six: readiness signs for solids often appear: steady head, sitting with support, interest in food, opening the mouth for a spoon, and moving food back instead of pushing it out with the tongue.

Chapter three. Senses and the growing brain.

Color vision is good, and depth perception is improving, so reaching gets more accurate. Babies start to recognize their name and respond to emotions in your voice.

Brain exercise for this month: cause and effect. Give your baby a rattle or a crinkly toy and let them discover that they make the sound. Play peekaboo, and narrate. Read every day.

The natural lens. Natural-parenting families often prefer real objects: a wooden spoon, a metal measuring cup, a soft cloth. Our reasoning: real objects have weight, texture, and temperature, and that variety is interesting. Always check for choking hazards: if it fits through a toilet-paper tube, it's too small.

Chapter four. Movement and tummy time.

Babies may roll both ways, pivot on their tummy, and push up on straight arms. Some rock on hands and knees later this month or next. Keep floor time generous. Avoid baby walkers; the AAP warns they cause injuries and don't help walking.

The natural lens. Barefoot floor play is the natural-movement default, and it's also mainstream: babies learn balance with their feet free.

Chapter five. Feeding, four ways, and first-foods planning.

Four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Many babies feed about five to eight times a day. Breast milk remains the main food. The 2023 Rios-Leyvraz and Yao review found intake around six months averaged about seven hundred thirty milliliters a day in exclusively breastfed babies, similar to three months.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. Bottles of about four to six ounces are common, a range borrowed from formula guidance.

Formula. The AAP describes about six to eight ounces per feed, four to five times a day, by around six months, usually not more than about thirty-two ounces a day.

Mixed feeding. Count measured bottles and breast feeds separately.

First-foods planning, the mainstream baseline. Around six months, babies' iron stores fall, so iron-rich first foods matter. The AAP, CDC, and the 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines list meat, poultry, seafood, eggs, and iron-fortified infant cereals among good options. The new Dietary Guidelines emphasize real, nutrient-dense foods and avoiding highly processed foods and added sugars. Pediatric researchers writing in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2026 criticized those guidelines for dropping specific guidance on fortified infant cereals, which remain a useful iron source for many babies.

The natural lens. Many functional medicine and traditional-diet voices, including the Weston A. Price Foundation, prefer meat, egg yolk, and later liver over cereal as first foods. There's research behind part of that. A 2006 randomized trial led by Dr. Nancy Krebs found meat was well accepted as a first food for breastfed babies and provided more zinc than iron-fortified cereal. There's also a contaminant concern with rice. The FDA set an action level for inorganic arsenic in infant rice cereal in 2020, and both the AAP and FDA suggest varying grains rather than relying on rice. Our reasoning: meat and egg are strong first foods; if you use cereal, choose iron-fortified oat or multigrain over rice-only.

What not to do. Don't start keto or carnivore diets for a baby. Babies need carbohydrate, fat, and protein, and breast milk itself is high in carbohydrate from lactose. The natural, nutrient-dense approach applies to which foods you offer, not cutting whole food groups. No honey before twelve months. No cow's milk as a drink before twelve months. No juice before twelve months. No added salt or sugar.

The parent's plate. Real food, protein, and enough of it. If you're low-carb and breastfeeding, keep eating enough and don't fast.

Chapter six. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Many babies take about three naps and sleep about twelve to fifteen hours in total. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months. Don't put your baby to bed with a bottle; that's linked to tooth decay once teeth arrive.

The natural lens. Our reasoning: a consistent morning wake time, daylight during the day, and a dim, quiet bedtime routine reinforce the body clock.

Chapter seven. Looking ahead.

By six months, the CDC lists rolling from tummy to back, pushing up with straight arms, leaning on hands while sitting, reaching to grab, blowing raspberries, laughing, recognizing familiar people, and closing lips to show they're done eating. Teething most often starts around six months; the bottom front teeth usually come first. Sitting alone falls between about four and nine months, crawling between about five and thirteen and a half months, and walking alone between about eight and eighteen months in the WHO motor study.

Chapter eight. What this means, and what to do.

First, watch for readiness signs; they matter more than the date.

Second, plan iron-rich first foods: meat, egg, and if you like, iron-fortified non-rice cereal.

Third, set up a safe high chair and learn the difference between gagging and choking. Consider an infant CPR class.

Fourth, keep honey, cow's milk as a drink, juice, and added salt and sugar off the menu.

Fifth, offer real objects to explore, checking size for choking safety.

When to call. Under three months, a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, means calling your pediatrician right away. From three to six months, the AAP says to call for a fever of one hundred one, or thirty-eight point three Celsius, or higher. Call too if your baby doesn't reach for things, doesn't respond to sounds, can't hold the head steady, or has lost a skill. In an emergency, call nine one one.

episodes.title: Month 6: First Tastes, Safely
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month six, from six to seven months, roughly weeks twenty-six through thirty: first tastes, safely. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This month at a glance.

Around six months, most babies are ready for solid foods, and that's the big change this month. Many babies also sit with support or briefly alone, roll both ways, reach and grab with ease, laugh, and babble. The first teeth often appear around now. The goal this month isn't to replace milk. It's to start practicing eating, safely, with nutrient-dense food.

Chapter two. Week by week this month.

Week twenty-six: if readiness signs are present, offer a first food once a day, when your baby is alert and not starving.

Week twenty-seven: try a new single food every few days. The CDC suggests waiting three to five days between new foods at first, so reactions are easier to spot.

Week twenty-eight: introduce common allergens like egg and peanut, in safe forms, if you haven't yet.

Week twenty-nine: offer water in an open cup with meals, a few sips at a time.

Week thirty: many babies move to two meals a day and start mashed or soft finger foods.

Chapter three. Senses and the growing brain.

Babies recognize familiar people and may be wary of strangers. They respond to their name and to emotions. Depth perception is developing well.

Brain exercise for this month: mealtimes as conversation. Sit with your baby, name foods, describe colors and textures, and smile. Eating together is a social skill. The CDC still recommends no screens before age two except video calls, and that includes during meals.

Chapter four. Movement and tummy time.

Many babies sit with support, lean on their hands to sit, and roll both ways. Some sit briefly alone. The WHO's motor study places sitting alone between about four and nine months. Keep floor time generous. Avoid baby walkers.

The natural lens. Free, barefoot floor play on a safe surface remains the natural-movement priority, and mainstream advice agrees.

Chapter five. Feeding, four ways, and first foods.

Four routes, kept separate. Breast milk or formula remains the main nutrition through the first year.

Feeding at the breast. Keep nursing on demand. Offer the breast before or around meals; solids start small.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. Bottles of about four to eight ounces are common, a range borrowed from formula guidance. You can mix expressed milk into foods.

Formula. The AAP describes about six to eight ounces per feed, four to five times a day, around six months. As solids increase, formula may decrease slightly.

Mixed feeding. Count measured bottles and breast feeds, and note solids separately.

First foods, the mainstream baseline. The AAP, CDC, WHO, and 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines recommend starting around six months with readiness signs, and offering a variety of nutrient-dense foods. Iron matters: meat, poultry, fish, eggs, beans, and iron-fortified cereals are all on the list. Introduce peanut and egg early, in safe forms. The LEAP trial showed early peanut introduction cut peanut allergy dramatically in high-risk babies. Serve peanut as thinned peanut butter or powder mixed into food, never whole nuts or spoonfuls of thick nut butter.

The natural lens. Traditional-diet voices, including the Weston A. Price Foundation, favor egg yolk, pureed meat, bone broth, and butter. The 2006 Krebs trial supports meat as a first food for breastfed babies. Current allergy guidance favors whole egg, white and yolk, when solids begin, not delaying egg white. Our reasoning: start with meat and egg, add vegetables and fruit, and use real fats like butter in cooking. Skip added salt, which the mainstream advises against for babies.

Purees or baby-led weaning? Baby-led weaning, popularized by Gill Rapley, skips purees and offers soft finger foods. A 2016 study from New Zealand, called BLISS, found babies following a modified, safety-focused baby-led approach didn't choke more than spoon-fed babies. Either approach can work, and many families mix both.

Safety lines. No honey before twelve months, because of infant botulism. No cow's milk as a drink before twelve months, though yogurt and cheese are fine. No juice before twelve months. About four to eight ounces of water a day is enough at this age, according to the AAP. Avoid choking hazards: whole grapes, nuts, popcorn, hard raw vegetables, and chunks of hard food. Always seat your baby upright and stay right there.

Teeth. When the first tooth appears, the AAP recommends brushing twice a day with a smear of fluoride toothpaste, about the size of a grain of rice. The natural lens: some families prefer fluoride-free toothpaste, and hydroxyapatite toothpastes are popular in this space. Research on hydroxyapatite is emerging; it's not yet the mainstream standard. Talk with your pediatrician or pediatric dentist.

The parent's plate. Many parents eat what they'd like their baby to eat. The 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines emphasize real food and protein. Babies should eat from the family table in a safe texture, not a keto or carnivore diet of their own.

Chapter six. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Many babies take two or three naps and sleep about twelve to fifteen hours in total. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months.

The natural lens. Our reasoning: daylight outdoors for the baby and a dim, calm bedtime help the body clock. After six months, the AAP says sunscreen is fine to use, but shade and clothing still come first.

Chapter seven. Looking ahead.

By nine months, the CDC lists sitting without support, getting to a sitting position alone, passing things from hand to hand, raking food with the fingers, babbling like mamama and bababa, looking for dropped objects, and lifting arms to be picked up. Crawling falls between about five and thirteen and a half months in the WHO study, and walking alone between about eight and eighteen months. More teeth will come over the coming months.

Chapter eight. What this means, and what to do.

First, start solids when readiness signs appear, around six months.

Second, lead with iron-rich foods: meat, egg, and other nutrient-dense options.

Third, introduce egg and peanut early, in safe forms.

Fourth, keep honey, cow's milk as a drink, juice, and added salt and sugar off the menu.

Fifth, brush the first teeth, and decide on toothpaste with your pediatrician or dentist.

When to call. After six months, the AAP says to call for a fever of one hundred three degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-nine point four Celsius, or higher, and sooner for any fever with a seizure, trouble breathing, a stiff neck, a rash that doesn't fade when pressed, signs of dehydration, or a baby who seems very ill. Teething does not cause a true fever. Call too for hives, swelling, vomiting, or trouble breathing after a new food; trouble breathing is an emergency, so call nine one one. Call too if your baby doesn't babble, doesn't respond to their name, or has lost a skill.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from the CDC, AAP HealthyChildren pages, the WHO, NIAID peanut guidelines, and the 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines. Studies named: LEAP 2015, Krebs 2006, and the BLISS choking study from 2016. The natural lens draws on the Weston A. Price Foundation. Natural-lens material names its source and is opinion or emerging evidence unless we said otherwise. Links are in the Sources tab. This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. See you in month seven.

episodes.title: Month 7: Textures and Sitting Tall
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month seven, from seven to eight months, roughly weeks thirty through thirty-four: textures and sitting tall. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This month at a glance.

Seven-month-olds are often sitting more steadily, reaching for everything, and exploring food with real enthusiasm, or real suspicion. Many have one or two teeth, many don't yet, and both are normal. Babies are learning that things exist even when out of sight, which makes peekaboo thrilling and separations harder.

Chapter two. Week by week this month.

Week thirty: many babies sit with less support and use their hands to play while sitting.

Week thirty-one: food textures can move from smooth to mashed and lumpy. Practice with texture now supports chewing skills later.

Week thirty-two: babies may rake small pieces of soft food toward themselves with the whole hand.

Week thirty-three: wariness with strangers may appear. It's a healthy sign of attachment.

Week thirty-four: some babies start rocking on hands and knees or scooting, early steps toward crawling.

Chapter three. Senses and the growing brain.

Depth perception is good now. Babies look for objects that fall and enjoy dropping things to watch them go. Babbling adds more consonants.

Brain exercise for this month: hide and find. Hide a toy under a cloth while your baby watches, then let them find it. Name objects and body parts. Read books with flaps. Respond to babbling as if it's conversation, because it is.

The natural lens. Montessori-inspired families often use an object-permanence box or a simple basket of real objects. The reasoning, giving babies real problems to solve, matches what we know about learning through play, though there's no evidence one toy beats another.

Chapter four. Movement and tummy time.

Many babies sit alone briefly, roll both ways, and pivot on their tummy. Crawling on hands and knees falls between about five and thirteen and a half months in the WHO motor study, and some babies skip crawling altogether. Give lots of floor time, and childproof now: cover outlets, secure furniture, and gate stairs.

The natural lens. Barefoot floor play is the natural-movement favorite and is also mainstream. Skip baby walkers; the AAP warns they cause injuries.

Chapter five. Feeding, four ways, and textures.

Four routes, kept separate. Breast milk or formula is still the main nutrition.

Feeding at the breast. Keep nursing on demand. Many babies nurse about four to six times a day plus night feeds, with solids added on top.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. Bottles of about six to eight ounces are common, a range borrowed from formula guidance. Some intake shifts to food over the coming months.

Formula. Many babies take about six to eight ounces, three to five times a day, depending on solids. The AAP suggests usually not more than about thirty-two ounces a day.

Mixed feeding. Count measured bottles, breast feeds, and solids separately.

Solids, the mainstream baseline. Most babies eat two to three small meals a day by now. The 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines list meat, poultry, seafood, vegetables, fruits, full-fat yogurt and cheese, whole grains, legumes, and nut- or seed-containing foods prepared safely. Offer iron-rich foods at least once a day. Choose low-mercury fish such as salmon, sardines, and cod.

The natural lens. Traditional-diet voices like the Weston A. Price Foundation suggest small amounts of liver after six months, along with bone broth and butter. Liver is extremely rich in iron, B12, and vitamin A. Our reasoning: small portions of liver, occasionally, can be part of a nutrient-dense diet, but because liver is so high in vitamin A, it shouldn't be a daily food or combined with cod liver oil or other vitamin A supplements without your pediatrician's input. The Foundation also favors raw cheese; the CDC and FDA warn that raw milk products carry a real risk of serious infection for babies, so choose pasteurized dairy.

Safety lines. No honey before twelve months. No cow's milk as a drink before twelve months, though yogurt and cheese are fine. No juice. About four to eight ounces of water a day. Avoid choking hazards like whole grapes, nuts, popcorn, raw carrots, and hot dogs in coins. Gagging is noisy and normal as babies learn; choking is silent and needs immediate action. An infant CPR class is worth it.

The parent's plate. Many parents eat along with their baby. If you're keto or carnivore yourself, offer your baby the nutrient-dense animal foods from your plate, but also fruits, vegetables, and grains; babies shouldn't follow a restrictive diet.

Chapter six. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Many babies take two or three naps and sleep about twelve to fifteen hours in total. Separation anxiety can disrupt sleep. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months.

The natural lens. Our reasoning: morning light, an outdoor walk, and a short, consistent bedtime routine help babies settle, especially during separation anxiety phases. Brief, calm reassurance at night is fine.

Chapter seven. Looking ahead.

By nine months, the CDC lists being shy or clingy with strangers, showing several facial expressions, looking when you call their name, reacting when you leave, smiling at peekaboo, babbling mamama and bababa, lifting arms to be picked up, looking for dropped objects, banging two things together, getting to sitting alone, moving things between hands, raking food with fingers, and sitting without support. Walking alone falls between about eight and eighteen months in the WHO study.

Chapter eight. What this means, and what to do.

First, move textures forward: from smooth to mashed and lumpy.

Second, offer an iron-rich food every day.

Third, if you use liver, keep it small and occasional, and avoid doubling up on vitamin A.

Fourth, childproof for crawling.

Fifth, learn gagging versus choking, and take a CPR class.

When to call. After six months, the AAP says to call for a fever of one hundred three degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-nine point four Celsius, or higher, and sooner for any fever with a seizure, trouble breathing, a stiff neck, a rash that doesn't fade when pressed, signs of dehydration, or a baby who seems very ill. Teething does not cause a true fever. Call too for hives, swelling, or vomiting after a new food, and call nine one one for any trouble breathing. Call if your baby isn't babbling, doesn't respond to their name, isn't trying to sit, or has lost a skill.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from the CDC, AAP HealthyChildren pages, the WHO, the FDA, and the 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines. The natural lens draws on the Weston A. Price Foundation's infant-feeding guide. Natural-lens material names its source and is opinion or emerging evidence unless we said otherwise. Links are in the Sources tab. This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. See you in month eight.

episodes.title: Month 8: On the Move
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month eight, from eight to nine months, roughly weeks thirty-four through thirty-nine: on the move. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This month at a glance.

Eight-month-olds are often on the move, crawling, scooting, rolling across the room, or pulling up on furniture. Many babies show separation anxiety: crying when a parent leaves. Hands are getting more precise, and many start picking up small pieces between thumb and fingers. Meals are becoming more like real meals.

Chapter two. Week by week this month.

Week thirty-four: many babies crawl or scoot. Some go straight from sitting to pulling up.

Week thirty-five: separation anxiety may peak. Short, warm goodbyes help more than sneaking out.

Week thirty-six: a pincer grasp, using the thumb and finger, starts emerging. Soft finger foods become easier.

Week thirty-seven: some babies pull to stand, holding furniture.

Week thirty-eight and thirty-nine: babbling becomes more varied, with strings like dadada and bababa, and babies may wave or clap with help.

Chapter three. Senses and the growing brain.

Vision is close to adult-like for many tasks. Babies follow your pointing, look where you look, and enjoy simple games.

Brain exercise for this month: point and name. Point at things, name them, and wait for your baby to look. Play pat-a-cake and simple songs with hand motions. Read books with real photos.

The natural lens. Natural-parenting families often spend more time outdoors as babies become mobile, with grass, sand, and leaves to explore under supervision. Our reasoning: varied textures and environments are good sensory input. Watch for small objects and anything that goes in the mouth.

Chapter four. Movement and tummy time.

Crawling on hands and knees falls between about five and thirteen and a half months in the WHO motor study, and standing with assistance between about five and eleven and a half months. Some babies never crawl in the classic way, and that can be fine. Give plenty of floor time and safe spaces to explore.

Childproofing: gate stairs, anchor furniture, cover outlets, lock cabinets with chemicals and medicines, and keep cords and small objects out of reach.

The natural lens. Barefoot is best for early movement, according to both natural-movement voices and the AAP. Shoes are for protection outdoors, not for learning to walk. Skip baby walkers.

Chapter five. Feeding, four ways, and meals.

Four routes, kept separate. Breast milk or formula is still the main nutrition through twelve months.

Feeding at the breast. Many babies nurse about three to five times a day plus any night feeds, with solids increasing.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. Bottles of about six to eight ounces are common. Start offering an open cup or straw cup with meals.

Formula. Many babies take about six to eight ounces, three to four times a day, depending on solids. The AAP suggests usually not more than about thirty-two ounces a day.

Mixed feeding. Count measured bottles, breast feeds, and solids separately.

Solids. Most babies eat two to three meals a day. Offer a variety: meat, fish, eggs, vegetables, fruits, full-fat yogurt and cheese, beans, and whole grains. Keep textures soft and appropriate, and move toward small, soft finger foods as the pincer grasp develops. Continue introducing allergens regularly once tolerated; repeated exposure helps maintain tolerance.

The natural lens. The 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines and functional medicine voices like Dr. Mark Hyman agree on one big point: avoid highly processed foods and added sugars. Many packaged baby snacks contain added sugars or refined starches. Our reasoning: real food from your table, cooked soft and unsalted, is usually the most nutrient-dense option.

Safety lines. No honey before twelve months. No cow's milk as a drink before twelve months; yogurt and cheese are fine. No juice. About four to eight ounces of water a day. Avoid choking hazards like whole grapes, nuts, popcorn, raw carrots, and hot dogs in coins.

The parent's plate. Eat with your baby when you can. Babies learn eating by watching. If you eat keto or carnivore, your baby can share the nutrient-dense animal foods, but should also get fruits, vegetables, and grains.

Chapter six. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Many babies take two naps and sleep about twelve to fifteen hours in total. Separation anxiety and new skills like pulling to stand can disrupt sleep for a few weeks. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months.

The natural lens. Our reasoning: a predictable routine, morning light, and active outdoor play during the day help babies fall asleep at night.

Chapter seven. Looking ahead.

By nine months, the CDC lists being shy or clingy with strangers, showing facial expressions, looking when you call their name, reacting when you leave, babbling mamama and bababa, lifting arms to be picked up, looking for dropped objects, banging things together, getting to sitting alone, and sitting without support. By twelve months: pulling to stand, cruising along furniture, waving, and picking things up with thumb and finger. Walking alone falls between about eight and eighteen months.

Chapter eight. What this means, and what to do.

First, childproof the house at crawling height.

Second, keep floor time generous and feet bare.

Third, offer an open cup or straw cup with meals.

Fourth, build meals from real food at your table, with no added salt or sugar.

Fifth, make goodbyes short and warm.

When to call. After six months, the AAP says to call for a fever of one hundred three degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-nine point four Celsius, or higher, and sooner for any fever with a seizure, trouble breathing, a stiff neck, a rash that doesn't fade when pressed, signs of dehydration, or a baby who seems very ill. Teething does not cause a true fever. Call too for any trouble breathing after a food, which means calling nine one one, or for hives or vomiting after a new food. Call if your baby isn't sitting with support, isn't babbling, doesn't respond to their name, or has lost a skill.
