episodes.title: Month 9: The Nine-Month Checkpoint
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month nine, from nine to ten months, roughly weeks thirty-nine through forty-three: the nine-month checkpoint. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This month at a glance.

Nine months is a checkpoint. The AAP recommends a standardized developmental screening at the nine-month well visit. The CDC's list of what most babies do by nine months includes: being shy, clingy, or fearful around strangers; showing several facial expressions; looking when you call their name; reacting when you leave; smiling or laughing at peekaboo; babbling like mamama and bababa; lifting arms to be picked up; looking for objects when dropped; banging two things together; getting to a sitting position alone; moving things from one hand to the other; using fingers to rake food; and sitting without support.

Chapter two. Week by week this month.

Week thirty-nine: many babies sit steadily and get in and out of sitting on their own.

Week forty: pulling to stand becomes common. Expect falls; keep the area padded and clear.

Week forty-one: babies may understand simple words like no and their own name.

Week forty-two: the pincer grasp improves. Small, soft finger foods are easier.

Week forty-three: many babies eat three meals a day plus breast milk or formula.

Chapter three. Senses and the growing brain.

Babies understand more than they can say. They follow pointing, look at named objects, and enjoy turn-taking games.

Brain exercise for this month: label everything. Name objects, people, and actions throughout the day. Ask simple questions: where's the ball? Wait for your baby to look or point. Read picture books every day.

The natural lens. Natural-parenting families often emphasize unstructured outdoor play. Our reasoning: open-ended exploration in a safe space supports curiosity and movement.

Chapter four. Movement and tummy time.

The WHO motor study found standing with assistance between about five and eleven and a half months, and walking with assistance between about six and fourteen months. Many babies cruise along furniture soon. Barefoot indoors helps balance.

The natural lens. Barefoot movement is a natural-movement principle that the AAP shares: babies learn to walk best barefoot indoors. Skip baby walkers and jumpers.

Chapter five. Feeding, four ways, and family meals.

Four routes, kept separate. Breast milk or formula remains important through twelve months.

Feeding at the breast. Many babies nurse three to five times a day, and some still nurse at night.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. Bottles of about six to eight ounces, or the same milk in an open or straw cup.

Formula. Many babies take about six to eight ounces, three to four times a day, usually not more than about thirty-two ounces a day.

Mixed feeding. Count measured bottles, breast feeds, and solids separately.

Family meals. Most babies eat three meals and one or two snacks. Offer soft, bite-size versions of family foods with no added salt or sugar. Include iron-rich foods daily: meat, fish, eggs, and beans.

The natural lens. The MAHA Report, released in May 2025, and the 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines both target ultra-processed foods and added sugars in children's diets. Our reasoning, consistent with both: cook simple, whole foods, and read labels on baby snacks. The FDA's Closer to Zero program is setting limits on lead and other contaminants in baby foods. Homemade baby food lets you control ingredients, though contaminants can also come from soil and produce, so variety matters.

Safety lines. No honey before twelve months. No cow's milk as a drink before twelve months; yogurt and cheese are fine. No juice. About four to eight ounces of water a day. Choose pasteurized dairy; the CDC warns raw milk products carry serious risks for babies. Avoid choking hazards like whole grapes, nuts, popcorn, raw carrots, and hot dogs in coins.

The parent's plate. Eat with your baby when you can. If your own diet is low-carb or carnivore, share the nutrient-dense animal foods, and give your baby fruits, vegetables, and grains too.

Chapter six. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Many babies take two naps and sleep about twelve to fourteen hours in total. Pulling to stand in the crib can disrupt sleep for a while. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months. Lower the crib mattress once your baby can pull to stand.

The natural lens. Our reasoning: morning daylight, active outdoor play, and a predictable bedtime help.

Chapter seven. Looking ahead.

By twelve months, the CDC lists playing games like pat-a-cake, waving bye-bye, calling a parent mama or dada or a special name, understanding no, putting things in a container, looking for things they saw you hide, pulling to stand, walking while holding furniture, drinking from a cup without a lid as you hold it, and picking things up between thumb and pointer finger. Walking alone falls between about eight and eighteen months in the WHO study.

Chapter eight. What this means, and what to do.

First, go to the nine-month visit with notes, and ask about the developmental screening.

Second, label everything, and read daily.

Third, lower the crib mattress if your baby is pulling to stand.

Fourth, build meals from simple whole foods, with no added salt or sugar.

Fifth, keep dairy pasteurized, and keep honey off the menu.

When to call. After six months, the AAP says to call for a fever of one hundred three degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-nine point four Celsius, or higher, and sooner for any fever with a seizure, trouble breathing, a stiff neck, a rash that doesn't fade when pressed, signs of dehydration, or a baby who seems very ill. Teething does not cause a true fever. Call nine one one for any trouble breathing after a food. Call your pediatrician if your baby isn't sitting without support, doesn't babble, doesn't respond to their name, doesn't look for dropped things, or has lost a skill.

episodes.title: Month 10: Cruising and First Gestures
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month ten, from ten to eleven months, roughly weeks forty-three through forty-seven: cruising and first gestures. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This month at a glance.

Ten-month-olds are often cruising along furniture, waving, clapping, and pointing. Many understand simple words and routines. Finger feeding is getting skilled, and family meals are becoming the norm. Some babies take a first independent step; many don't for months yet, and both are normal.

Chapter two. Week by week this month.

Week forty-three: cruising, walking sideways while holding furniture, is common.

Week forty-four: waving bye-bye and clapping may appear, often copied from you.

Week forty-five: pointing at things they want or find interesting is a big communication step.

Week forty-six: drinking from an open cup with help, or a straw cup, gets easier.

Week forty-seven: some babies stand alone briefly. Walking alone falls between about eight and eighteen months in the WHO motor study.

Chapter three. Senses and the growing brain.

Babies are building language fast. They understand far more words than they say, follow simple routines, and use gestures to communicate.

Brain exercise for this month: gesture and word together. When you wave, say bye-bye. When you point, name it. When your baby points, respond: yes, that's a dog. Read every day, and let your baby turn pages.

The natural lens. Natural-parenting families often add simple sign language for words like more, all done, and milk. There's little strong evidence that baby sign speeds speech, but it doesn't delay it, and many families find it reduces frustration. We label that as low-cost, low-risk reasoning.

Chapter four. Movement and tummy time.

Cruising strengthens balance and leg muscles. Give your baby safe furniture to hold, a push toy that's stable, and lots of floor time. Barefoot indoors helps.

The natural lens. Barefoot walking is a natural-movement principle the AAP also supports for learning to walk. Skip baby walkers and jumpers; the AAP warns walkers cause injuries.

Chapter five. Feeding, four ways, and family foods.

Four routes, kept separate. Breast milk or formula is still important until twelve months.

Feeding at the breast. Many babies nurse about three to four times a day, often around waking and sleep.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle or cup. Many babies take expressed milk in an open or straw cup. The AAP recommends moving off bottles between about twelve and eighteen months, so practicing cups now helps.

Formula. Many babies take about six to eight ounces, three to four times a day, usually not more than about thirty-two ounces in total.

Mixed feeding. Count measured bottles or cups, breast feeds, and solids separately.

Family foods. Most babies eat three meals and one or two snacks. Offer soft, bite-size pieces of family meals with no added salt or sugar. Include iron-rich foods every day.

The natural lens on baby food contaminants. A 2021 U.S. House report raised concerns about heavy metals in commercial baby foods, and the FDA's Closer to Zero program has since set guidance for lead in processed baby foods. The MAHA movement has pushed these issues to the front. Our reasoning: a varied diet, homemade foods when possible, and limiting rice-based snacks reduce exposure to any single source. Contaminants can be in soil and produce too, so variety matters more than any single brand.

The natural lens on fats. Traditional-diet voices recommend cooking with butter, tallow, olive oil, or coconut oil rather than industrial seed oils. The new Dietary Guidelines emphasize healthy fats and full-fat dairy. The seed-oil debate itself is unsettled; we label it as an open question. Babies need plenty of fat for brain growth, so full-fat foods are the default either way.

Safety lines. No honey before twelve months. No cow's milk as a drink before twelve months. No juice. About four to eight ounces of water a day. Pasteurized dairy only. Avoid choking hazards like whole grapes, nuts, popcorn, raw carrots, and hot dogs in coins.

Chapter six. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Many babies take two naps and sleep about twelve to fourteen hours in total. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months.

The natural lens. Our reasoning: daylight in the morning, active outdoor play, and a dim, calm bedtime routine. A consistent wake time helps the body clock more than an early bedtime alone.

Chapter seven. Looking ahead.

By twelve months, the CDC lists playing games like pat-a-cake, waving bye-bye, calling a parent mama or dada or a special name, understanding no, putting something in a container, looking for things they saw you hide, pulling to stand, walking while holding furniture, drinking from a cup without a lid as you hold it, and picking things up with thumb and pointer finger. By fifteen months, the CDC lists taking a few steps alone, and by eighteen months, walking without holding on.

Chapter eight. What this means, and what to do.

First, pair gestures with words all day.

Second, practice open-cup and straw-cup drinking.

Third, keep meals varied, homemade when you can, and low in rice-based snacks.

Fourth, keep feet bare indoors and skip walkers.

Fifth, keep honey, cow's milk as a drink, juice, and added salt and sugar off the menu until the first birthday, and added sugar well beyond.

When to call. After six months, the AAP says to call for a fever of one hundred three degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-nine point four Celsius, or higher, and sooner for any fever with a seizure, trouble breathing, a stiff neck, a rash that doesn't fade when pressed, signs of dehydration, or a baby who seems very ill. Teething does not cause a true fever. Call nine one one for any trouble breathing after a food. Call your pediatrician if your baby isn't babbling, doesn't respond to their name, doesn't use gestures, or has lost a skill.

episodes.title: Month 11: Almost One
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month eleven, from eleven to twelve months, roughly weeks forty-seven through fifty-two: almost one. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This month at a glance.

Eleven-month-olds are often standing, cruising, and maybe taking first steps. Many say a first word, like mama, dada, or a special name. They understand simple directions and love to imitate. Families start planning for the transition at twelve months: from formula to whole milk, from bottles to cups, and from baby foods to family foods.

Chapter two. Week by week this month.

Week forty-seven: many babies stand alone briefly. The WHO motor study places standing alone between about seven and seventeen months.

Week forty-eight: first steps may come, often between furniture or toward you. Many babies don't walk alone until well after their first birthday, and that's normal.

Week forty-nine: first words may appear. Babies also use gestures and sounds to communicate.

Week fifty: babies may follow simple directions with gestures, like give me the ball.

Week fifty-one and fifty-two: planning the twelve-month transition.

Chapter three. Senses and the growing brain.

Babies understand many words and routines, imitate actions, and enjoy simple pretend play, like feeding a doll.

Brain exercise for this month: expand. When your baby says a word or makes a sound, expand it: ball, yes, a big red ball. Read every day, and let your baby choose the book.

The natural lens. Natural-parenting families often prefer simple, open-ended toys like blocks, balls, and containers. Our reasoning: open-ended play invites imagination. There's no strong evidence that any toy is better, so cost and simplicity can guide you.

Chapter four. Movement and tummy time.

Walking alone falls between about eight and eighteen months in the WHO motor study. The CDC lists taking a few steps alone by fifteen months and walking without holding on by eighteen months. So a baby who isn't walking at the first birthday is well within the normal range.

The natural lens. Barefoot walking indoors is a natural-movement principle that the AAP also supports. Shoes are for protection outdoors; choose flexible soles. Skip baby walkers; the AAP warns they cause injuries and may delay walking.

Chapter five. Feeding, four ways, and the twelve-month transition.

Four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Many babies nurse about two to four times a day. The AAP and WHO support continuing breastfeeding as long as mother and baby want, to two years or beyond.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle or cup. Offer it in an open or straw cup. The AAP recommends moving off bottles between about twelve and eighteen months.

Formula. Many babies take about six to eight ounces, three to four times a day. The 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines and the AAP say formula can stop at twelve months, with whole milk as the main milk drink.

Mixed feeding. Count measured cups or bottles, breast feeds, and solids separately.

Planning whole milk. From twelve to twenty-four months, the AAP's drinks guidance suggests about sixteen ounces, or two cups, of whole milk a day. Too much milk can crowd out iron-rich foods. Water: about one to four cups a day.

The natural lens on milk. Many families in the natural and MAHA space prefer organic or grass-fed whole milk, and some want raw milk. The CDC, FDA, and AAP strongly advise against raw milk for children, because it can carry bacteria that cause severe illness. Our reasoning: pasteurized, whole, grass-fed or organic milk satisfies the natural preference without the infection risk.

Family foods. Offer three meals and two snacks. Include protein foods like meat, fish, and eggs, plus vegetables, fruits, full-fat dairy, and whole grains or legumes. No added salt or sugar.

Safety lines. No honey until after twelve months. Avoid choking hazards like whole grapes, nuts, popcorn, raw carrots, and hot dogs in coins.

Chapter six. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Many babies take one or two naps and sleep about eleven to fourteen hours in total. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months.

The natural lens. Our reasoning: morning daylight, outdoor play, and a predictable bedtime help, as always. Screens aren't recommended before age two, and that includes before bed.

Chapter seven. Looking ahead.

By twelve months, the CDC lists playing games like pat-a-cake, waving bye-bye, calling a parent mama or dada or a special name, understanding no, putting something in a container, looking for hidden things, pulling to stand, walking while holding furniture, drinking from a cup without a lid as you hold it, and picking things up with thumb and pointer finger. By fifteen months: a few steps alone, and trying to say one or two words besides mama and dada.

Chapter eight. What this means, and what to do.

First, celebrate first words and first steps, and don't worry if they haven't come yet.

Second, plan the twelve-month switch: whole milk about sixteen ounces a day, cups instead of bottles.

Third, choose pasteurized milk.

Fourth, keep feet bare indoors and skip walkers.

Fifth, expand on every word your baby says.

When to call. After six months, the AAP says to call for a fever of one hundred three degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-nine point four Celsius, or higher, and sooner for any fever with a seizure, trouble breathing, a stiff neck, a rash that doesn't fade when pressed, signs of dehydration, or a baby who seems very ill. Teething does not cause a true fever. Call your pediatrician if your baby isn't pulling to stand, doesn't use gestures like waving or pointing, doesn't babble, or has lost a skill. In an emergency, call nine one one.

episodes.title: Month 12: One Year!
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month twelve: one year. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This month at a glance.

Happy first birthday. In one year, your baby has gone from reflexes to reaching, crawling or scooting, pulling up, and maybe walking. From crying to babbling, gestures, and maybe first words. From milk only to family meals. This episode covers the twelve-month checkpoint, the transition to toddler eating, and what's coming next.

Chapter two. Week by week this month.

Week one: the twelve-month well visit. Bring your notes and questions.

Week two: switching from formula to whole milk, if you use formula, and moving from bottles to cups.

Week three: honey can now be introduced, in small amounts. Added sugar is still best avoided.

Week four: many babies are walking, cruising, or close. Some aren't yet, and that's fine.

Chapter three. Senses and the growing brain.

By twelve months, the CDC lists playing games like pat-a-cake, waving bye-bye, calling a parent mama or dada or a special name, understanding no, putting something in a container, and looking for things they saw you hide.

Brain exercise for this month: talk, read, play. Narrate your day, expand on your toddler's words, read every day, and play simple pretend games. The CDC recommends no screen time before age two except video calls.

The natural lens. Natural-parenting families often emphasize outdoor play and real-world experiences. Our reasoning: variety, movement, and responsive adults are what toddlers need, and outdoor time supports that.

Chapter four. Movement.

By twelve months, the CDC lists pulling to stand and walking while holding furniture. The WHO motor study places walking alone between about eight and eighteen months. The CDC lists walking without holding on by eighteen months.

The natural lens. Barefoot walking indoors, as both natural-movement voices and the AAP recommend. Flexible shoes for outdoors.

Chapter five. Feeding, four ways, and toddler eating.

Four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. The AAP and WHO support continuing breastfeeding as long as mother and child want, to two years or beyond. Breast milk continues to provide nutrition and immune factors.

Pumped breast milk in a cup. Offer it in an open or straw cup. The AAP recommends moving off bottles between about twelve and eighteen months.

Formula. The AAP and the 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines say formula can stop at twelve months, switching to whole cow's milk. Toddler formulas aren't necessary for most children.

Whole milk. From twelve to twenty-four months, the AAP's drinks guidance suggests about sixteen ounces of whole milk a day. More can crowd out iron-rich foods. Water: about one to four cups a day.

The natural lens on milk. Organic or grass-fed whole milk is a reasonable choice. Raw milk isn't. The CDC, FDA, and AAP strongly advise against raw milk for children because of the risk of serious infection.

Toddler eating, the mainstream baseline. The 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines emphasize real, nutrient-dense foods: protein foods like meat, poultry, seafood, and eggs, plus vegetables, fruits, full-fat dairy, whole grains, and legumes. Avoid highly processed foods and added sugars.

The natural lens. Functional medicine and traditional-diet voices, from Dr. Mark Hyman to the Weston A. Price Foundation, emphasize real food, animal protein, healthy fats, and avoiding ultra-processed foods and added sugars. That overlaps strongly with the new Dietary Guidelines. What we don't recommend is a keto or carnivore diet for a toddler. Toddlers need carbohydrates from fruits, vegetables, and grains for energy and fiber. Our reasoning: build toddler meals around nutrient-dense animal foods if that's your family's style, but always include fruits, vegetables, and grains.

Safety lines. Honey is now okay. Avoid choking hazards like whole grapes, nuts, popcorn, raw carrots, and hot dogs in coins until at least age four. Keep foods soft and bite-size.

Chapter six. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Many toddlers take one or two naps and sleep about eleven to fourteen hours in total. Safe sleep still matters: a firm, flat crib with no pillows, blankets, or bumpers.

The natural lens. Our reasoning: morning daylight, outdoor play, and a calm, predictable bedtime routine without screens help sleep.

Chapter seven. Looking ahead.

By fifteen months, the CDC lists taking a few steps alone, trying to say one or two words besides mama and dada, looking at a familiar object when you name it, and showing you affection. By eighteen months: walking without holding on, trying to say three or more words, and following simple directions without gestures. The AAP recommends developmental screening at eighteen months, and autism-specific screening at eighteen and twenty-four months.

Chapter eight. What this means, and what to do.

First, celebrate. You made it through the first year.

Second, plan the milk switch: whole milk around sixteen ounces a day, cups instead of bottles.

Third, keep milk pasteurized.

Fourth, build toddler meals from real, nutrient-dense foods, including fruits, vegetables, and grains.

Fifth, keep talking, reading, and playing every day.

When to call. After six months, the AAP says to call for a fever of one hundred three degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-nine point four Celsius, or higher, and sooner for any fever with a seizure, trouble breathing, a stiff neck, a rash that doesn't fade when pressed, signs of dehydration, or a baby who seems very ill. Teething does not cause a true fever. Call your pediatrician if your child isn't pulling to stand, doesn't use gestures like waving or pointing, doesn't say any words by fifteen months, or has lost a skill. In an emergency, call nine one one.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from the CDC, AAP HealthyChildren pages, the WHO, the FDA, and the 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines. The natural lens draws on Dr. Mark Hyman and the Weston A. Price Foundation. Natural-lens material names its source and is opinion or emerging evidence unless we said otherwise. Links are in the Sources tab. This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. Thank you for listening to Little Steps through the first year.
